# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (circa 1800, before statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview

In 1800, the area that would become Alabama was divided between **two governing authorities**:

- **Mississippi Territory** (est. 1798): controlled the interior and northern portions following the U.S. acquisition of the region
- **Spanish Mobile District**: Spain retained Mobile and the Gulf Coast until 1813

The full jurisdictional sequence:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Notes |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| 1702–1763 | French (Mobile District) | French colonial records |
| 1763–1780 | British (West Florida) | British colonial records |
| 1780–1813 | Spanish (Mobile District) | Spanish colonial records for Gulf Coast |
| 1798–1817 | Mississippi Territory (US) | American records begin for interior |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory | Separated from Mississippi Territory |
| 14 Dec 1819 | State of Alabama | State-level records begin |

**Economy:** Subsistence farming and the fur trade in 1800; cotton cultivation expanded rapidly after 1814. Mobile was an active port.

**Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations (dominant in the interior); American settlers arriving from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia; French Creole and Spanish Creole populations around Mobile; a rapidly growing enslaved African American population.

**Religious denominations:** Catholic Church (Mobile, from the French period); Baptist congregations appearing in northern Alabama ca. 1808–1810; Methodist circuit riders; early Presbyterian presence.

**Key events:** Creek War (1813–1814) opened northern Alabama to mass migration; Battle of Mobile (1813) transferred the Gulf Coast from Spain to the U.S.; Alabama Territory formed 1817; statehood December 14, 1819.

---

## Boundary changes

**This is the single most critical research issue for 1800.** Records for your ancestor were created under the Mississippi Territory (or, for Mobile-area families, under Spanish authority), *not* under "Alabama." Searching only Alabama-labeled collections will miss most pre-1817 evidence.

- Records for the interior before 1817 → search **Mississippi Territory** collections
- Records for Mobile and the Gulf Coast before 1813 → search **Spanish colonial** sources
- County-level records begin only when Alabama counties were formed (from **1809 onward**)
- Any record labeled "Alabama" before December 1819 is strictly a territorial record

When the Mississippi Territory split in 1817, records created during the territorial period were eventually divided between Mississippi and Alabama repositories. Some Mississippi Territory records relevant to Alabama settlers remain in Mississippi-scoped collections at FamilySearch and NARA.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Alabama did **not** require statewide registration of births, marriages, and deaths until **1908**. There are no civil vital records for 1800.
- **What exists for marriages:** Individual county marriage registers begin as early as **1809** (at the earliest Alabama county formations). FamilySearch holds [Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408) — 612,345 indexed records with 306,172 images. ✅ **Indexed + images**
- **Gaps:** No birth or death registration before 1908. Nothing for vital events in 1800 itself.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records, probate files (which name heirs), and census/tax records are the only sources for family relationships before 1908.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, 1702+); Baptist (northern Alabama, ca. 1808+); Methodist circuit riders; Presbyterian (later).
- **FamilySearch collection:** [Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396) — 156,789 records with 78,394 images. ✅ **Indexed + images**
- **Catholic Mobile records:** The Diocese of Mobile Archives and the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception hold registers dating from the French colonial period. The Mobile Municipal Archives holds microfilm of French colonial church registers.
- **Spanish colonial church records:** Spanish church registers for the Mobile District are held at the **Archivo General de Indias** in Seville, with copies at the **Library of Congress** (per FamilySearch Wiki, "Alabama Genealogy," Colonial Records section).
- **Language:** Catholic records from the French/Spanish period are in Latin, French, or Spanish — plan for translation.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1800 and 1810 federal censuses covered the Mississippi Territory, including present-day Alabama. The 1800 coverage is fragmentary; the **1810 census** is the first reasonably complete enumeration of Alabama-area settlers.
- **Territorial censuses (critical):** The Mississippi Territory conducted enumerations in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** covering present-day Alabama. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ("Alabama Genealogy," Territorial Records section), these are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery. These are the most important census-type sources for 1800.
- **FamilySearch (Alabama scope):** [Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756) — 287,634 indexed records; ⚠️ **index only, no images online** (images must be accessed through original repositories).
- **FamilySearch (Mississippi scope):** [Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171) — 198,340 records, no images — may include territorial-era enumerations covering the Alabama portion. ⚠️ **Index only; confirm whether Alabama-area entries are included.**

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, inventories, guardianships — critical for establishing family relationships before vital registration.
- **FamilySearch (Alabama):** [Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764) — 438,210 records with 219,105 images. ✅ **Indexed + images.** These begin at county formation (1809+).
- **FamilySearch (Mississippi Territory):** [Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293) — 245,670 records, 122,835 images — covers the territorial period when Alabama-area courts operated under Mississippi Territory jurisdiction. ✅ **Indexed + images.** Search this collection for pre-1817 records.
- **Physical holdings:** Early probate files are at individual county courthouses (Alabama) and at ADAH. Pre-1809 territorial court records are at NARA and ADAH.

### Land records
- **System:** Alabama is a **federal land state** (public domain). The federal government distributed land through the General Land Office (GLO) — patents are the primary first-title documents, not state grants.
- **Federal patents:** Searchable free online at the **BLM General Land Office Records** website (glorecords.blm.gov), searchable by name.
- **Private land claims:** Settlers holding pre-American (Spanish or British) land grants had to file "private land claims" with the U.S. government. These are in federal records at NARA and are essential for Mobile-area families.
- **FamilySearch (Mississippi Territory scope):** [Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694) — 312,450 records, 156,225 images — covers the territorial period. ✅ **Indexed + images.** Verify whether the Alabama portion of the territory is represented.
- **Deed books:** After county formation (1809+), deed books are at county courthouses.
- **Spanish land grants:** Spanish land records for the Mobile District are at the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville) with copies at the Library of Congress (per FamilySearch Wiki, Colonial Records section).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812 (Battle of Mobile, 1813); territorial militia service (1798+).
- **Record types:** Militia muster rolls, service records, pension files, bounty land warrants.
- **Repository:** Pension files and service records are at **NARA**; accessible via Fold3 (subscription). Militia rolls for the Mississippi Territory are at NARA and ADAH.
- **External link (from FamilySearch curated resources):** [Fold3 – Military Records](https://www.fold3.com/)

### Cemetery records
- **Online:** [FindAGrave](https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Alabama cemeteries, including older rural and church burial grounds. Coverage for pre-1820 marked graves is sparse — headstones from this period are rare.
- **Physical:** Early church cemeteries associated with Baptist and Methodist congregations may hold informal burial registers; most are at local churches or county historical societies.

### Newspaper records
- **Availability:** Alabama's earliest newspapers began in the late territorial period. The *Mobile Gazette* (Mobile) was among the first. Most interior Alabama newspapers postdate statehood (1819).
- **Where held:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) and ADAH hold historical Alabama newspaper collections. Coverage for the year 1800 is essentially nonexistent.
- **Practical value for 1800:** Minimal. Legal notices, estate notices, and land-sale notices become useful once newspapers begin appearing in the 1815–1820 range.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county tax lists (property, poll/personal).
- **Date range:** Alabama county tax records begin with county formation (1809+). Mississippi Territory tax records may begin as early as 1798.
- **Where held:** County tax records at individual courthouses and ADAH; territorial-level records at NARA and ADAH.
- **Substitute value:** ⭐ Tax lists are the most important census substitute for **1800–1810**, the period before reliable federal census coverage of Alabama-area settlers. Search these aggressively.

### Colonial records (pre-1798, Mobile area)
These are essential for Gulf Coast families and for any settler whose origins predate American control:
- **French records (1702–1763):** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France; microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Include census returns, church registers, land concessions.
- **British records (1763–1780):** Colonial Office records at The National Archives, Kew (UK). Covers the British West Florida period.
- **Spanish records (1780–1813):** Archivo General de Indias, Seville (PARES digital portal); copies at the Library of Congress. Include census returns (*padrones*), church registers, land grants for the Mobile District. If your ancestor was in Mobile before 1813, **these are primary sources.**

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama County Marriages 1809–1950 (612K indexed + images); Alabama Probate Records 1809–1985 (438K indexed + images); Alabama Census Substitutes 1810–1890 (288K, index only); Alabama Church Records 1803–1950 (157K indexed + images) | Free |
| FamilySearch (MS scope) | Mississippi Territorial & State Land Records 1798–1907 (312K indexed + images); Mississippi County Court Records 1799–1920 (246K indexed + images); Mississippi Compiled Census Substitutes 1792–1890 (198K, index only); Mississippi Church Records 1800–1950 (88K indexed + images) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Alabama federal land patents | Free |

| Fold3 | Military service records, pension files, War of 1812 | Subscription |

| PARES (Spain) | Spanish colonial records, Archivo General de Indias | Free (partial) |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH)**, Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); early county records; militia rolls; state archives | In-person; finding aids at archives.alabama.gov |
| **NARA** (Atlanta region & Washington DC) | Federal census microfilm; federal land entry files; military pension files; private land claims | In-person; some digitized via Fold3/Ancestry |
| **Individual county courthouses** (Alabama) | Deed books, probate files, marriage registers (from county formation date) | In-person / mail |

| **Mobile Municipal Archives**, Mobile, AL | French colonial microfilm; Mobile history records | In-person |
| **Library of Congress**, Washington DC | Copies of Spanish colonial records (Mobile District); French colonial documents | In-person; some digitized |

| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records (Mobile District, 1780–1813) | In-person; partial online via PARES |
| **The National Archives**, Kew, UK | British West Florida colonial records (1763–1780) | In-person / online (Discovery catalogue) |

---

## Records NOT online

- **Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808):** Held at ADAH; not fully digitized or indexed online. Plan a visit or contact ADAH.
- **Pre-1809 Mississippi Territory court records (Alabama portion):** Mostly physical at NARA and ADAH.
- **Spanish colonial land grants and church registers:** Partially digitized at PARES (Spain), but most require specialist access; copies at Library of Congress are not fully online.
- **French colonial church registers:** Microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives; originals in France.
- **Early county tax lists (pre-1820):** Many survive only in physical form at county courthouses or ADAH.
- **British West Florida records (1763–1780):** Primarily at The National Archives, Kew.

---

## Known record losses

- **Sparse infrastructure in 1800:** Most of present-day Alabama was frontier in 1800. Many births, deaths, and even marriages went entirely unregistered — the records were never created, not merely lost.
- **Creek War disruption (1813–1814):** Some early records may have been lost or abandoned during the conflict.
- **Courthouse fires:** Several Alabama county courthouses suffered 19th-century fires. ADAH maintains loss documentation; always check which records survive before concluding a gap is total.
- **Spanish record removal (1813):** Some records were taken or transferred when Spain vacated Mobile; completeness of surviving Mobile District records varies.

---

## Research tips

1. **Search Mississippi Territory first.** Any ancestor in present-day Alabama in 1800 was legally in the Mississippi Territory. Use FamilySearch and NARA collections scoped to the Mississippi Territory — not "Alabama" — for the 1798–1817 period.

2. **Mobile area = Spanish sources until 1813.** If your ancestor was near Mobile or the Gulf Coast, the primary records before 1813 are Spanish colonial. Start with the Library of Congress's copies of Archivo General de Indias holdings, and check the PARES portal.

3. **Alabama is a federal land state.** The BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) is the starting point for land patents — free, searchable by name, and often the earliest document placing an ancestor in a specific location.

4. **Tax lists are your 1800–1810 census substitute.** The first reliable census for Alabama-area settlers is 1810. County and territorial tax lists at ADAH substitute for the gap. Search them as a first priority.

5. **Know your ancestor's county — and its formation date.** No county-level records pre-date county formation. If a county was formed in 1818, there are no county records before 1818; look to the Mississippi Territory level for anything earlier.

6. **The Creek War (1813–1814) is a genealogical boundary.** Most families who appear in Alabama records after 1815 migrated from the Carolinas, Virginia, or Georgia following the Creek War. If you lose the trail in Alabama, trace the family back through those states' records first.

7. **Consult the FamilySearch Wiki article "Alabama Genealogy"** (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy) — it provides county-by-county formation dates and detailed guidance on record availability, and was the source for the territorial census and colonial record details in this guide.

# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region (Pre-1800, Spanish Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **European contact:** Hernando de Soto's expedition, 1541; first permanent European settlement, Arkansas Post (Fort de la Rivière des Cadodaquious), established by the French in 1686
- **Sovereignty timeline:**
  - **French Louisiana** (1686–1763): La Louisiane; Arkansas Post administered from New Orleans
  - **Spanish Louisiana** (1763–1800): ceded to Spain by the Treaty of Paris (1763); Arkansas Post became a Spanish colonial garrison and the administrative hub of the entire Arkansas district
  - **French Louisiana (briefly)** (1800–1803): secretly retroceded to France by the Treaty of San Ildefonso (1800)
  - **United States** (1803–): Louisiana Purchase; region organized as the District of Arkansas under the Territory of Orleans (1804), then Missouri Territory (1812), then Arkansas Territory (1819), and finally the State of Arkansas (1836)
- **Administrative center during target period:** Arkansas Post (present-day Arkansas County), the only organized European settlement and the seat of Spanish colonial authority for the entire region
- **Population:** No FamilySearch population data is available for this pre-statehood period. Settlement was sparse — a small French Creole and Spanish garrison population, with a few hundred colonists in the Arkansas Post area. No broader civil infrastructure existed outside the Post.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence agriculture, and military garrison supply
- **Ethnic/national composition:** French Creole settlers (long-established), Spanish colonial administrators and soldiers, a small number of Anglo-American traders, and significant Native American populations (Quapaw, Osage, and others)
- **Religion:** Roman Catholic — the only institutional church present; administered under the Diocese of Louisiana and the Floridas (based in New Orleans)
- **Key events:** Spanish takeover (1763–69 transition), periodic Quapaw treaty negotiations, American Revolution border skirmishes (1770s–80s), Spanish land concession campaigns to attract settlers (1780s–90s)

---

## Boundary changes

The region had no county structure before 1813. The entire modern state of Arkansas fell within the vast, undivided administrative jurisdiction of **Spanish Louisiana**, headquartered at New Orleans, with Arkansas Post as the only organized sub-district. Records created before 1803 were made under Spanish (and before 1763, French) colonial authority — not under any U.S., territorial, or county government. Any search of U.S.-era Arkansas county records will find nothing for this period; researchers must pivot entirely to colonial-era and ecclesiastical repositories. The earliest county-level U.S. records for the region begin with Arkansas County (formed 1813 from Missouri Territory).

---

## Available record types

### Church / sacramental records (primary source for vital events)

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — for European settlers, soldiers, and sometimes Native Americans
- **What FamilySearch holds:**
  - **1 digitized volume** — Image Group **008814402**: *Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post*, covering **1763–1800**
  - 64 images · Language: **Spanish** · `recordSearchablePercent`: **0%** · `fulltextSearchable`: **false**
  - ⚠️ **Browse-only images** — must be examined page by page; there is no name index and no full-text search. The researcher must also be able to read Spanish, including colonial ecclesiastical Latin/Spanish script.
- **Earlier French-era registers (pre-1763):** French Catholic missionary registers from the early 1700s onward survive in part. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ("Arkansas Genealogy — Church Records"), these are held by the **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** and in transcribed form at the **Arkansas History Commission**. These are **not on FamilySearch** and must be requested from those repositories directly.
- **Access note:** The Diocese of Little Rock Archives can be contacted for access to pre-1763 registers. The Arkansas History Commission (AHC) holds transcriptions.

---

### Spanish colonial censuses (*padrones*)

- **What they are:** Periodic population enumerations (*padrones*) conducted by Spanish colonial authorities at Arkansas Post, recording heads of household and family members, often with ages, origins, and occupations
- **FamilySearch coverage:** No indexed collection covers this record type. The `collections_search` for Arkansas filtered to 1686–1803 returned **zero collections overlapping the colonial period** (the three collections returned all begin in 1819 or later). This is a significant digitization gap.
- **Where held:**
  - **Arkansas History Commission (AHC), Little Rock** — the primary repository for surviving Arkansas Spanish colonial civil records, per the FamilySearch Wiki ("Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records")
  - **Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville, Spain** — the central archive of the Spanish colonial empire; holds the official colonial administrative correspondence, censuses, and land records for Louisiana and its sub-districts, including Arkansas Post
  - **Library of Congress, Washington, D.C.** — holds microfilm copies of selected AGI materials relating to Louisiana and the Gulf South
- **Access:** Physical visit or correspondence with AHC; the AGI has a partial online catalog (PARES portal, pares.mcu.es) but most Arkansas-relevant documents are not yet digitized. Library of Congress microfilm can be ordered through interlibrary loan.

---

### Land concessions / grants

- **System:** Spanish colonial land grants (*concesiones*), not the later U.S. rectangular survey system
- **What they contain:** Grantee name, land description, witnesses, date; often the only civil record documenting a settler's presence in the district
- **Spanish land grant confirmations:** After the Louisiana Purchase, the U.S. government required holders of Spanish and French land grants to file confirmation claims. These U.S.-era confirmation records (post-1803) are accessible and often name the original colonial grantee — a valuable backdoor into the pre-1800 period.
  - **U.S. Confirmation records** are held at the **National Archives (NARA)** and the General Land Office / Bureau of Land Management (BLM)
- **Colonial-era originals:** Held at **AHC** (Little Rock) and the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville)
- **FamilySearch:** No digitized or indexed collection for Spanish colonial Arkansas land grants was returned by the survey tools.

---

### Military post records

- **Context:** Arkansas Post was a Spanish military garrison throughout 1763–1800. Muster rolls, officer reports, and correspondence were generated at the post.
- **Where held:** The **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville) and its Louisiana section; some materials microfilmed and held at the **Library of Congress**; the **AHC** (Little Rock) holds transcriptions and some originals
- **FamilySearch:** No digitized military records for this period and place appeared in the survey.

---

### Civil vital records

- **Not applicable for this period.** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in Spanish colonial Arkansas. The Church was the sole recorder of vital events (see Sacramental Records above).

---

### Census records (U.S.-era substitutes beginning 1819)

- The earliest U.S. enumeration data for the region comes after the colonial period. FamilySearch holds **"Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870"** (Collection ID: 2085124, 178,345 indexed records) — this begins in 1819 and is **outside** the target window, but it can help confirm the post-colonial survival and descent of colonial families.

---

### Probate and court records

- **No Spanish colonial-era probate or civil court records** were returned by the survey tools for this period. Any formal proceedings would have gone through Spanish colonial civil courts at Arkansas Post or been appealed to New Orleans. Surviving records, if any, would be at **AHC** or the **AGI**.

---

### Newspapers

- **None for this period.** No newspapers were published in the Arkansas region before 1800.

---

### Immigration / emigration

- **No formal passenger records** for colonial Arkansas. Movement into the region was by river (the Arkansas and Mississippi) and was not formally documented in the way Atlantic port arrivals were. Settler arrivals may appear in Spanish colonial censuses, land concessions, or church sacramental registers.

---

### Online repositories

| Repository | Holdings for this place & period | Access |

| FamilySearch | 1 browse-only volume: Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial) 1763–1800, 64 images, in Spanish, Image Group 008814402 | Free — browse image-by-image |
| AGI PARES portal (pares.mcu.es) | Partial catalog of Archivo General de Indias; some Louisiana colonial documents viewable online | Free to search; limited digitization |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | U.S.-era land patent confirmations of Spanish grants (post-1803) — may name original colonial grantees | Free |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |

| **Arkansas History Commission (AHC)**, Little Rock, AR | Spanish colonial civil records, padrones, land concessions, transcriptions of French/Spanish church registers | In-person or written inquiry; contact: history.arkansas.gov |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock Archives** | French-era sacramental registers (pre-1763 baptisms, marriages, burials) | Contact the Diocesan Archives directly |
| **Archivo General de Indias (AGI)**, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial administrative records for Louisiana (including Arkansas Post): censuses, military rosters, land concessions, judicial proceedings | In-person; remote consultation through the PARES portal |
| **Library of Congress**, Washington, D.C. | Microfilm of selected AGI Louisiana records | In-person or interlibrary loan through a FHL affiliate |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Post-1803 U.S. confirmation records of Spanish and French land grants in Arkansas | In-person (Washington, D.C.); some available online via Fold3 |

---

## Records NOT online

The following record classes for the Spanish colonial period are **not** available in any online database per this survey:

- Spanish colonial censuses (*padrones*) of Arkansas Post
- French and Spanish Catholic registers predating 1763 (Diocese of Little Rock / AHC physical only)
- Spanish colonial land concession originals
- Spanish colonial military muster rolls and post records
- Any colonial-era court or probate proceedings

The single FamilySearch digitized volume (Image Group 008814402, sacramental registers 1763–1800) is online but **not indexed** — it must be browsed image-by-image in Spanish.

---

## Known record losses and gaps

- Settlement in the Arkansas region before 1800 was overwhelmingly concentrated at Arkansas Post. Records for the wider region simply were not created — there was no administrative presence outside the Post.
- The colonial period predates U.S. county formation entirely. Searching FamilySearch's Arkansas county collections will yield nothing for pre-1800 events.
- An unknown portion of colonial records was lost in the transitions between French, Spanish, and American administrations. The most complete surviving corpus is at the AGI in Seville.
- No population data exists in FamilySearch's system for this pre-statehood period.

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with the one digitized volume on FamilySearch.** Image Group 008814402 (Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers, 1763–1800, Spanish, browse-only) is the most accessible primary source. Browse all 64 images; it covers baptisms, marriages, and burials through the entire Spanish colonial period.
2. **Work backward from U.S.-era land confirmations.** After 1803, colonial land-grant holders had to file confirmation claims with the U.S. government. This is a critical substitute source.
3. **Contact the Arkansas History Commission first.** The AHC in Little Rock is the principal repository for colonial-era Arkansas records and can direct you to transcriptions, microfilm, and finding aids without a trip to Seville.

6. **Records are in Spanish (and sometimes French or Latin).** All colonial records require reading 18th-century Spanish or French. Consider engaging a professional translator or paleographer familiar with colonial Louisiana documents.
7. **The compiled census substitutes index (FamilySearch Collection 2085124, 1819–1870)** begins after the colonial period but may help trace descendants of colonial families and confirm continuity of settlement.

# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region (Pre-1800, Spanish Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **European contact:** Hernando de Soto, 1541; Arkansas Post established by the French in 1686 (first European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley)
- **Sovereignty timeline:**
  - French Louisiana (1686–1763)
  - Spanish Louisiana (1763–1800) — Treaty of Paris (1763)
  - French Louisiana briefly (1800–1803) — Treaty of San Ildefonso
  - United States (1803–) — Louisiana Purchase; District of Arkansas / Missouri Territory / Arkansas Territory (1819) / State of Arkansas (1836)
- **Administrative center during target period:** Arkansas Post (present-day Arkansas County) — the only organized European settlement and seat of Spanish colonial authority
- **Population:** No FamilySearch data available. Settlement was sparse — a small French Creole and Spanish garrison population at Arkansas Post; no civil infrastructure outside the Post.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence agriculture, military garrison supply
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish colonial administrators/soldiers, a small number of Anglo-American traders, significant Native American populations (Quapaw, Osage)
- **Religion:** Roman Catholic only, administered under the Diocese of Louisiana and the Floridas (New Orleans)
- **Key events:** Spanish takeover (1763–69 transition), Spanish land concession campaigns to attract settlers (1780s–90s)

## Boundary changes

No county structure existed before 1813. The entire modern state of Arkansas fell within undivided Spanish Louisiana, administered from New Orleans with Arkansas Post as sub-district hub. U.S. county records begin only with Arkansas County (formed 1813). Searching FamilySearch's Arkansas county collections yields nothing for pre-1800 events — researchers must use colonial repositories.

## Available record types

### Church / sacramental records (primary source for vital events)

- **What FamilySearch holds:** 1 digitized volume — Image Group **008814402**: *Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, 1763–1800*; 64 images; language: **Spanish**; `recordSearchablePercent`: 0%; `fulltextSearchable`: false
- ⚠️ **Browse-only images** — must be examined page by page with no name index and no full-text search; requires reading Spanish/colonial Latin script
- **French-era registers (pre-1763):** held by the **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock Archives** and in transcribed form at the **Arkansas History Commission (AHC)** — not on FamilySearch

### Spanish colonial censuses (padrones)

- Periodic population enumerations recording heads of household, family members, ages, origins, occupations
- **Not digitized or indexed on FamilySearch** — zero collections overlap the 1686–1803 window
- Held at: **AHC (Little Rock)**, **Archivo General de Indias (Seville)** — searchable via pares.mcu.es, **Library of Congress** (microfilm)

### Land concessions / grants

- Spanish colonial land grants (*concesiones*) — often the only civil record documenting a settler's presence
- **Post-1803 U.S. confirmation records** (BLM GLO / NARA) frequently name the original colonial grantee — a critical backdoor into the pre-1800 period
- Colonial originals: **AHC** and **Archivo General de Indias**
- Not digitized on FamilySearch for this period

### Military post records

- Arkansas Post was a Spanish garrison; muster rolls, officer reports, and correspondence were generated
- Held at **AGI (Seville)** and **AHC (Little Rock)**; some microfilmed at **Library of Congress**
- Not digitized on FamilySearch

### Civil vital records

- **Not applicable.** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in Spanish colonial Arkansas. The Church was the sole recorder of vital events.

### Census records (post-colonial substitutes)

- FamilySearch Collection 2085124, *Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870* (178,345 indexed records) — begins 1819, outside the colonial window, but useful for tracing descending families

### Newspapers / probate / court records

- No newspapers published in the region before 1800
- Colonial-era probate/court proceedings, if any, would be at AHC or AGI; none returned by survey tools

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Image Group 008814402: Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial) 1763–1800, 64 images, Spanish, browse-only | Free |
| AGI PARES portal (pares.mcu.es) | Partial catalog of Archivo General de Indias; some Louisiana colonial documents viewable | Free to search |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | U.S.-era land patent confirmations of Spanish/French grants (post-1803) | Free |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission (AHC), Little Rock | Spanish colonial civil records, padrones, land concessions, church register transcriptions | In-person or written inquiry: history.arkansas.gov |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock Archives | French-era sacramental registers (pre-1763) | Contact diocesan archives |
| Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records for Louisiana incl. Arkansas Post | In-person; PARES portal for catalog/scans |
| Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. | Microfilm of selected AGI Louisiana records | In-person or interlibrary loan via FHL |
| NARA | Post-1803 U.S. confirmation records of Spanish/French land grants | In-person; some on Fold3 |

## Records NOT online

- Spanish colonial censuses (padrones)
- French and Spanish Catholic registers predating 1763
- Spanish colonial land concession originals
- Spanish colonial military muster rolls and post records
- Colonial-era court/probate proceedings

The single FamilySearch digitized volume (Image Group 008814402) is online but **not indexed** — browse-only.

## Known record losses and gaps

- Settlement before 1800 was overwhelmingly concentrated at Arkansas Post; records for the wider region were simply not created
- The colonial period predates U.S. county formation entirely; FamilySearch Arkansas county collections return nothing for this period
- An unknown portion of colonial records was lost in the French–Spanish–American transitions; the most complete surviving corpus is at the AGI in Seville

5. **Records are in Spanish, French, or Latin** — engage a professional translator or paleographer familiar with colonial Louisiana documents
6. **FamilySearch Wiki 'Arkansas Genealogy'** — the wiki_search confirmed a dedicated 'Colonial Records' section and 'Church Records' section at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy
7. **The compiled census substitutes index (Collection 2085124, 1819–1870)** can help trace descendants of colonial families after the colonial period ends

# 📍 Locality Research Guide: Ohio (Pre-Statehood), ~1790
**Jurisdiction at the time:** Northwest Territory, United States (1787–1803)
**Ohio statehood:** March 1, 1803
**Target period:** ~1770–1810 (centered on 1790)

---

## 1. Jurisdictional History & Boundary Changes

In 1790, **Ohio did not yet exist as a state or even a named territory of its own.** The region was governed under the **Northwest Territory**, created by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. This single fact is the most important thing a researcher must understand: all records created before 1803 were generated under territorial (not state) authority, and often under only two county governments.

### County Formation Timeline (Critical for Record Location)

| County | Organized | Parent | Notes |
|--------|-----------|--------|-------|
| **Washington County** | 1788 | Northwest Territory | First county; covered most of eastern/southeastern Ohio |
| **Hamilton County** | 1790 | Washington County | Covered most of southwestern Ohio |
| *(All other Ohio counties)* | 1798–1820s | Washington or Hamilton | Carved progressively after statehood |

> **Research rule:** For any event in Ohio before ~1800, determine whether the location fell within Washington County or Hamilton County at that time — those were the only two courts generating records. An event recorded in what is today Adams, Pike, or Ross County was almost certainly filed in **Hamilton County** (if SW Ohio) or **Washington County** (if SE/E Ohio). After statehood, those parent-county records are the continuous research trail into the territorial era — treat them as one connected record set, not as separate repositories.

### Land District Overlay (Affects Survey Systems and Record Repositories)

Ohio had **three overlapping land systems** in 1790, each with its own records and holding repositories:

| District | Location | Survey System | Records Held At |
|----------|----------|---------------|-----------------|
| **Virginia Military District** | Between Scioto & Little Miami rivers | Metes-and-bounds (irregular) | Virginia State Library (Richmond); Ohio History Connection |
| **Connecticut Western Reserve** | Northeastern Ohio strip | Township-range grid (Connecticut-style) | Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland |
| **Federal (BLM) Lands** | Remainder of Ohio | U.S. Public Land Survey (township-range) | BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) |

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy — Land Records")*

---

## 2. Records Available & Access Levels

### 🟢 Land Records — **Best Pre-Statehood Source**

**Why land records matter in 1790:** Land is the primary documented event for settlers in this era. No civil vital registration existed; courts were minimal. But land transactions left paper trails.

- **FamilySearch collection:** [Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187) (collection ID 1542187) — **234,567 indexed records / 117,283 images** — name-searchable online.
- **Territorial Land Records volume** (image group 005112233): 51 images covering **Northwest Territory, 1788–1799** — **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable** — must be browsed image by image with no keyword search capability.
- **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov): Federal land patents for public-domain Ohio lands — free, searchable online.
- **Virginia Military District warrants:** At the **Virginia State Library** (Richmond) for Revolutionary War veteran grants in SW Ohio.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve:** At the **Western Reserve Historical Society** (Cleveland) for NE Ohio settlers.

### 🟡 Marriage Records — **Partial Coverage Starting 1789**

- **FamilySearch collection:** [Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785) (collection ID 1803785) — **1,523,678 records / 761,839 images** — name-searchable.
- Coverage for 1789–1803 is limited to **Washington and Hamilton counties** only, reflecting the two organized governments of the era. Do not expect to find marriages from later-formed counties before those counties existed.

### 🟡 Church Records — **Often the Only Vital Record Source**

No civil birth or death registration existed anywhere in Ohio in 1790. Church registers (baptism, marriage, burial) are frequently the **sole documentation** of vital events in this period.

- **FamilySearch collection:** [Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917) (collection ID 2246917) — **678,234 records / 339,117 images** — name-searchable.
- Denominations active in early Ohio settlements: Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, Quaker (Friends), and German Reformed/Lutheran in areas settled by German-speaking migrants.
- Physical originals may be held at individual congregation archives or deposited with denominational historical societies.

### 🔴 Tax Records — **Starts 1800, Not 1790**

- **FamilySearch collection:** [Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542) — **345,890 records** — starts in 1800, one decade after the target year.
- **Washington County tax records volume** (image group 005112240): 73 images, 1799–1803, **12% name-indexed** — most must be browsed.
- For the year 1790 itself, no digitized tax records are available on FamilySearch. The **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus) holds territorial-era tax lists that may not yet be digitized.

### 🔴 Death Records — **Does Not Exist for 1790**

- **FamilySearch collection:** [Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1417891) — starts **50 years after the target period**. Entirely irrelevant to 1790 research.
- **Gap strategy:** Use burial records (church registers, cemetery transcriptions on FindAGrave), probate/estate inventories at the county courthouse, and obituaries in early newspapers.

### 🟡 Military Records — **Revolutionary War Era**

- Many Ohio settlers of the 1780s–1790s were Revolutionary War veterans. Their **pension and bounty-land warrant files** at NARA are a rich source of biographical and family data.
- **Fold3.com** holds digitized Revolutionary War pension files — searchable by name.
- **NARA** (archives.gov) holds service records, pension files, and warrant applications.

### 🟡 Federal Census — **1790 Covers Northwest Territory, But Sparsely**

- The **1790 U.S. Federal Census** enumerated the Northwest Territory, but Ohio settlement was extremely sparse at that date — primarily the Marietta (Washington County) and Cincinnati (Hamilton County) settlements. Coverage is thin.
- The **1800 census** is more useful: it covers a broader settled population and is fully indexed online (Ancestry.com, FamilySearch).

### ⬜ Vital Registration — **Does Not Exist**

Ohio did not begin mandatory civil registration of births and deaths until **1867**. There are no birth or death certificates for 1790. Church records and probate estate files are the primary substitutes.

---

## 3. Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|-----------|--------------|--------|
| **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus) | Territorial court records, early county records, state archives | In-person; some microfilm via FamilySearch |
| **Western Reserve Historical Society** (Cleveland) | Connecticut Western Reserve land & family records | In-person; some digitized |
| **Virginia State Library** (Richmond) | Virginia Military District warrants | In-person; some online |
| **BLM General Land Office** | Federal land patents | Free online: glorecords.blm.gov |
| **NARA** (Washington, D.C. / regional) | Military service, pension, naturalization records | In-person + Fold3/Ancestry |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Marriages (1789+), land (1787+), church records (1787+) | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Census (1790, 1800, 1810), military records | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave.com** | Cemetery transcriptions and burial records | Free online |

---

## 4. Critical Research Quirks for This Period

1. **Always identify the 1790 county first.** Before searching any record, determine whether the location of interest was in **Washington County** or **Hamilton County** at that date. Records labeled under later county names don't exist yet — work from the parent county backward.
2. **Virginia Military District records are in Virginia, not Ohio.** If your ancestor held land between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers, the original warrant is at the Virginia State Library, not Ohio archives.
3. **Land records are the backbone.** With no civil vital registration and only two county courts, the land entry is often the earliest document placing an ancestor in Ohio.
4. **The 1790 census is sparse for Ohio.** Settlement was confined to Marietta and Cincinnati-area communities. If you don't find your ancestor in 1790, search the 1800 census — many settlers arrived between those dates.
5. **Church records pre-date or supplement county records.** For births, deaths, and marriages not captured by the two early county courts, the congregation register is the fallback — check Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, and Quaker records specifically.
6. **Tax lists substitute for censuses.** The 1799–1803 Washington County tax volume (image group 005112240, 12% indexed, largely browse-only) can serve as a near-census substitute for that area's male heads of household.
7. **Post-1803 county records continue the trail.** When a new county was formed after statehood from Washington or Hamilton, the earlier records remain in the parent county's books — don't search only the later county's records.

---

## 5. Digitization Summary

| Record Type | Period Available | FamilySearch Access Level | Notes |
|------------|-----------------|--------------------------|-------|
| Land Records | 1787–1840 | ✅ Indexed + images (234K records) | BLM GLO also free online |
| Territorial Land Records | 1788–1799 | ⚠️ Browse-only (51 images, 0% indexed) | Northwest Territory volume |
| County Marriages | 1789–2013 | ✅ Indexed + images (1.5M records) | Only Washington & Hamilton pre-1803 |
| Church Records | 1787–1950 | ✅ Indexed + images (678K records) | Primary vital record substitute |
| Tax Records | 1800–1850 | ✅ Indexed + images (346K records) | Starts 1800, not 1790 |
| Washington Co. Tax | 1799–1803 | ⚠️ Partially indexed (12%, 73 images) | Browse-mostly |
| Death Records | 1840–2001 | ✅ Indexed | Entirely postdates 1790 |
| Military (RevWar) | ~1775–1800 | ✅ Indexed (Fold3/NARA) | Pension files are rich |
| Federal Census | 1790, 1800 | ✅ Indexed (Ancestry/FS) | 1790 Ohio coverage is thin |
| Civil Birth/Death Reg. | — | ❌ Does not exist before 1867 | Church records are the substitute |

---

**Bottom line for 1790 Ohio research:** Your primary tools are **land records** (FamilySearch collection 1542187 + BLM GLO), **church records** (collection 2246917), and early **county marriage records** (collection 1803785) — all anchored to either **Washington County** or **Hamilton County**, the only two governments that existed in 1790. Military pension files at NARA are invaluable for settler-veterans. Civil vital registration simply did not exist; the gap is real and must be bridged through church registers, probate estate files, and cemetery records.

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1865)
### Gold Rush Migration & Settlement

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Statehood:** September 9, 1850 — California bypassed territorial status entirely, going directly from Mexican cession (Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, February 1848) to U.S. statehood
- **Pre-statehood authority:** Mexican California; prior to 1821, Spanish colonial California
- **Capital:** Sacramento (from 1854); Vallejo and Benicia briefly served earlier
- **County formation:** 27 original counties organized at statehood in 1850; many were subdivided as population grew through the decade
- **Population:** The Gold Rush (triggered January 24, 1848, at Sutter's Mill) drew approximately **300,000 migrants** from the rest of the United States and abroad by the mid-1850s — one of the most rapid demographic explosions in American history (Wikipedia, *California Gold Rush*)
- **Economy:** Placer and hard-rock gold mining, port commerce at San Francisco, agriculture in the Central Valley, supply and merchant trades serving mining camps
- **Ethnic composition:** Extraordinarily diverse — Anglo-American "forty-niners," Mexican Californios, Chilean and Peruvian miners, Chinese immigrants (especially from Guangdong Province), French, German, Irish, Australian, Hawaiian, and native Californians
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant through the mission era and among Californio/Mexican population), Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Congregational (arriving with American settlers), and early Jewish congregations in San Francisco
- **Key events:** Gold discovery 1848; California statehood 1850; California State Census 1852; Foreign Miners' Tax laws (1850, 1852) targeted Chinese and Latin American miners; San Francisco fires (1849–1851); transcontinental telegraph 1861; Civil War (California Volunteers organized 1861–1865)

---

## Boundary Changes

- California had no territorial phase — it entered the Union directly in 1850
- The original 27 counties of 1850 were subdivided repeatedly during the 1850s as mining camp populations stabilized into towns (e.g., Tulare, Fresno, and Plumas counties were carved from larger originals). **Always identify the county your ancestor lived in for the specific year in question**, as records created before a subdivision are held by the parent county
- Spanish/Mexican land grant records (the *ranchos*) were adjudicated by the U.S. Board of Land Commissioners, 1851–1856. Rancho-era records predate American county organization and are held separately (see Land Records below)

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Births:** California did **not** require statewide registration of births until **1905**. For the 1850s, birth documentation is sparse and county-level only. FamilySearch holds **California, County Births, 1850–1919** (collection 2017276; 789,456 records) — coverage is uneven across counties for the early decades
- **Marriages:** County-level marriage recording began at statehood (1850). FamilySearch holds **California, County Marriages, 1850–1952** (collection 1452832; 567,890 records / 1,135,780 persons)
- **Deaths:** No statewide death registration until 1905. Death documentation for the 1850s relies on church burial registers, cemetery records, probate files, and newspaper notices
- **Access:** Both county births and marriages collections are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch (free)
- **Gap:** Statewide death registration is entirely absent for this period. Seek substitutes in church records, cemetery records, and newspaper obituaries

### Church Records

- **Roman Catholic:** The most extensive institutional records in California before 1850. FamilySearch holds **California, Mission Records, 1769–1850** (collection 1804372; 98,765 records) covering baptisms, marriages, and burials at the Franciscan missions. These records are in Spanish and Latin. While they predate the main Gold Rush window, they document the Californio/Mexican families your migrant ancestors may have encountered or married into
- **Protestant denominations** (Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Congregational): Arrived with American settlers beginning 1849. Registers are scattered across individual church and denominational archives — no comprehensive FamilySearch collection exists for the 1850s. The **Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley)** and **California State Library** hold manuscript collections that include some congregation records
- **Chinese community:** Buddhist and Taoist temples and clan associations maintained their own records; the **Chinese Historical Society of America** (San Francisco) and **California State Library** hold relevant materials
- **Language note:** Catholic mission and early parish records are in Spanish or Latin; Chinese community records are in Chinese (Cantonese characters)

### Census Records

| Census | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **U.S. Federal Census 1850** | First federal enumeration in California — but **partially destroyed**; returns for several counties are missing entirely | Remaining counties indexed + images on Ancestry (subscription) and FamilySearch (free) |
| **California State Census 1852** | State-mandated enumeration filling the gap left by 1850 destruction — this is often the **most important single source** for Gold Rush researchers | **88% indexed + full-text searchable** on FamilySearch (volume 006601001; 522 images) |
| **U.S. Federal Census 1860** | Complete California coverage | Indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| **Mortality Schedules 1850, 1860** | List persons who died in the year preceding each census — valuable given the absence of death registration | Indexed on Ancestry; images on FamilySearch |

⚠️ **Critical gap:** The 1850 federal census for California is partially destroyed. The **1852 state census** is the essential substitute and should always be searched first for people present in California in the early 1850s.

### Gold Rush–Specific Records

These sources are especially important for tracing miners and migrants and have no equivalent in other states:

| Record Type | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Mining Claim Registers** | San Francisco, 1849–1855 (volume 006601002; 340 images) | ⚠️ **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image |
| **Port Arrival Registers, Sacramento** | 1849–1858 (volume 006601003; 298 images) | ⚠️ **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable |
| **Foreign Miners' Tax Records** | Monthly tax levied on non-citizen miners (1850 and 1852 acts); some county tax records survive | Physical only — held at individual county recorders' offices and California State Archives |
| **Great Registers (voter registration)** | Begin **1866**, just outside the target window, but capture many men who arrived during the Gold Rush and remained in California. FamilySearch collection 1923340 (1,345,678 records, 1866–1910) | Indexed on FamilySearch (free) |

Note: There are **14 digitized volumes** on FamilySearch for California in this period; the survey retrieved 3 from the first page. Additional volumes covering other counties and record types likely exist — browse FamilySearch's California catalog directly for the full list.

### Land Records

- **System:** California is a **federal public land state** — the rectangular survey system (townships/ranges) applies to most land. Spanish/Mexican-era *rancho* grants are a separate system
- **Bureau of Land Management (BLM) General Land Office (GLO):** Federal land patents are free and searchable at **glorecords.blm.gov** — essential for homesteaders and settlers who acquired federal land. Covers the 1850s
- **Spanish/Mexican Land Grants (Ranchos):** Adjudicated by the U.S. Board of Land Commissioners (1851–1856) and then the federal courts. Records are held at the **Bancroft Library** and **California State Archives**. The National Archives (NARA) Pacific Region (San Bruno) also holds related case files
- **Mining Claims:** Recorded at the county level by county recorders' offices. These are among the most direct evidence of a miner's presence. The San Francisco Mining Claim Registers (006601002) cover 1849–1855 but are browse-only
- **County Deed Records:** County courthouses hold deed books from 1850. Many have not been digitized

### Probate and Court Records

- **Probate:** Filed at the county level from 1850. Wills, estate inventories, and letters of administration name heirs and often identify where the deceased was from. Probate files for Gold Rush–era miners are especially rich — personal property inventories describe mining tools, claims, and cash
- **Court records:** Naturalizations (pre-1906) were filed in any court of record — Superior Courts, District Courts, county courts. **No single online database covers California naturalizations of the 1850s**; check county courthouse records and the California State Archives
- **Access:** Most probate and court records from the 1850s are **physical only** — held at county courthouses or transferred to the California State Archives. Some counties have produced name indexes

### Immigration and Arrival Records

- **Ship Passenger Manifests — San Francisco:** The single most important immigration source. Hundreds of thousands arrived by sea via the Cape Horn route or the Panama crossing. Manifests are held at the **National Archives, Pacific Region, San Bruno (NARA San Bruno)**, and are also indexed on **Ancestry.com** and **FamilySearch**. Full manifest images appear on Ancestry
- **Overland Arrivals:** No equivalent federal manifest exists for overland emigrants arriving via the California Trail. Sources include overland trail diaries (California State Library, Bancroft Library), county arrival registers, and newspaper notices
- **Naturalization:** Declarations of intention ("first papers") and final naturalization petitions from 1850s California were filed in county courts. No centralized index — search county by county
- **Passenger list note:** Examine full manifest pages, not just indexed entries — family members including infants and children traveling with parents appear on the same manifest page

### Military Records

- **Mexican-American War veterans (ended 1848):** Pension files and bounty land warrants at NARA; indexed on **Fold3** (subscription)
- **California Volunteers (Civil War, 1861–1865):** Service records and pension files at NARA; index on Fold3 and FamilySearch
- **California Militia (1850s):** Muster rolls at the California State Archives (not digitized)
- **Access:** NARA military records are available via **Fold3** (subscription) and some collections on FamilySearch (free)

### Newspaper Records

- California had active newspaper publishing from 1846. Gold Rush–era papers carried **obituaries, legal notices, mining news, ship arrival lists, and letters to the editor** — invaluable for locating individuals
- Key titles: *Alta California* (San Francisco, 1849+), *Sacramento Union* (1851+), *Daily Placer Times* (1849)
- **Access:** **Newspapers.com** (subscription) and the **California Digital Newspaper Collection** (cdnc.ucr.edu — free) hold digitized California newspapers. The California State Library holds microfilm of titles not yet online
- **Research value:** Newspaper notices of mining claim disputes, estate sales, and arrival announcements can document a person's presence when no official record exists

### Cemetery Records

- **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com — free) covers many California cemeteries including historic Gold Rush–era burying grounds
- **BillionGraves** (billiongraves.com) provides additional coverage
- Historic Gold Rush mining camp cemeteries are often undocumented or only partially transcribed — the **California State Library** and local county genealogical societies may hold sexton records and burial registers not yet online

### Tax Records

- County property and personal property tax rolls survive from 1850 for many counties. These are an important substitute for missing census years and can document miners' equipment and claims
- Held at county assessors' offices and the California State Archives; mostly **physical only**
- Foreign Miners' Tax receipts (1850, 1852) survive in scattered county collections — worth checking at the county recorder for mining counties (El Dorado, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Amador, Nevada, Placer)

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Key Collections for This Place & Period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | County Births 1850–1919 (789K records); County Marriages 1850–1952 (568K records); Mission Records 1769–1850 (99K records); Great Registers 1866–1910 (1.35M records); State Census 1852 (88% indexed); Mining Claim Registers 1849–1855 (browse-only); Port Arrival Registers 1849–1858 (browse-only) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1850, 1860); San Francisco passenger manifests; California vital records; newspapers | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military service records, pension files, Mexican-American War and California Volunteers | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Gold Rush–era California newspapers (*Alta California*, *Sacramento Union*, others) | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | California cemetery records statewide | Free |
| **BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov)** | Federal land patents in California | Free |
| **California Digital Newspaper Collection** (cdnc.ucr.edu) | Digitized California newspapers, including Gold Rush era | Free |
| **NARA Online (archives.gov)** | Federal records finding aids; some digitized passenger lists | Free / some restricted |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA** | San Francisco ship passenger manifests 1848–1900s; federal court records including naturalizations; federal land case files | In-person / FOIA requests |
| **California State Archives, Sacramento** | State census 1852; militia records; Spanish/Mexican land grant case files; state court records; some county transfers | In-person; some finding aids online |
| **California State Library, Sacramento** | Gold Rush manuscript collections; newspaper microfilm; genealogical reference materials; overland trail diaries | In-person; some digital collections |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Largest collection of Spanish/Mexican land grant records; Gold Rush diaries, letters, and photographs; Mexican California documents | In-person by appointment |
| **County Courthouses (El Dorado, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Amador, Nevada, Placer, Sacramento counties)** | Deed records; probate files; naturalization records; marriage registers; mining claim records | In-person / mail |
| **Chinese Historical Society of America, San Francisco** | Records of Chinese immigrant community, Tong records, clan association materials | In-person |

---

## Records NOT Online

The following record types exist for this period but are **not available in any online database** — do not assume they are lost:

- **County death records** (no statewide registration until 1905; sporadic county-level records physical only)
- **Foreign Miners' Tax receipts and registers** (county recorders' offices)
- **County personal property and poll tax rolls**
- **California Militia muster rolls** (California State Archives)
- **Pre-1906 naturalization records** from county courts (must search county by county)
- **Spanish/Mexican land grant original case files** (Bancroft Library and NARA San Bruno)
- **Local church registers** (Protestant denominations — held by individual churches or diocesan archives, largely undigitized)
- Most county **probate case files** (held at county courthouses; not systematically digitized)

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1850 U.S. Federal Census:** Partially destroyed — returns for several California counties are missing entirely. The **1852 California State Census** (88% indexed on FamilySearch) is the primary substitute
- **San Francisco Earthquake and Fire (1906):** While outside the target period, the 1906 disaster destroyed many San Francisco county records held through to that date. Records created in the 1850s that survived to 1906 may have been lost then. The loss affects vital records, naturalization files, and court records filed in San Francisco County
- **Mining camp impermanence:** Records created in temporary mining camps (Justice of the Peace records, informal claim registers) are largely lost — no organized custody, and camps were often abandoned

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1852 California State Census, not the 1850 federal census.** The 1852 census is better preserved, more complete for California, and captures the peak Gold Rush population. It is 88% name-indexed on FamilySearch

2. **Work backward from the Great Register.** Although voter registration (Great Registers) begins in 1866, many men who arrived during the Gold Rush appear — they list birthplace, age, occupation, and physical description. Use them to confirm identity and build a profile, then search backward into the 1850s records

3. **Identify your ancestor's mining county.** The Gold Rush was concentrated in the Sierra Nevada foothills (the "Mother Lode" counties: El Dorado, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Amador, Nevada, Placer). Mining claim registers, tax rolls, and court records are held at those specific county courthouses — general California-wide searches will miss them

4. **Search ship passenger manifests at NARA San Bruno or Ancestry.** If your ancestor arrived by sea (Cape Horn or Panama route), the San Francisco arrival manifests are the most direct proof of migration. Examine the full page for accompanying family members

5. **Check the Foreign Miners' Tax records** for immigrant ancestors. The 1850 and 1852 tax laws targeted Chinese, Mexican, Chilean, and other foreign-born miners. Some county tax receipt books survive and may be the only direct record of an immigrant miner's presence

6. **The Bancroft Library is indispensable for Spanish/Mexican California families.** If your research touches Californio families or the rancho system, no repository comes close to the Bancroft's holdings

7. **Browse the Mining Claim Registers image by image.** FamilySearch volume 006601002 (San Francisco Mining Claim Registers, 1849–1855, 340 images) is entirely unindexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed page by page. The same applies to the Port Arrival Registers (volume 006601003, 298 images)

8. **California's ethnic diversity means records are multilingual.** Catholic records may be in Spanish or Latin; Chinese community records are in Cantonese. Spanish-language records are particularly important for Californio families predating the Gold Rush

9. **Check newspaper archives early.** Gold Rush–era California newspapers are unusually rich. The *California Digital Newspaper Collection* (free, cdnc.ucr.edu) and Newspapers.com both cover this period and can document arrivals, disputes, and deaths that no official record captured

10. **14 digitized FamilySearch volumes** cover California in this period — only 3 are described above (the first page of results). Browse the full California catalog on FamilySearch for additional volumes covering specific counties and record types

---

*Sources: FamilySearch collections search and volume search (California, 1848–1865); FamilySearch Wiki, "California Genealogy — Gold Rush Records" and "Pre-Statehood Records" sections; Wikipedia, "California Gold Rush."*

# Locality Guide: New York City, Colonial Period (1700–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **City established:** 1624/1626 as New Amsterdam (Dutch colony); seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York
- **Administrative center:** New York City (Manhattan/New York County), seat of New York Province under British colonial rule
- **Parent jurisdiction during period:** New York Province (British Crown colony), 1664–1783. The State of New York was not formed until 1788, so all records created before 1784 belong to the provincial/colonial framework
- **Population during period:** No formal census data is available for this period from FamilySearch's data holdings; the city was estimated at approximately 5,000–25,000 inhabitants through the 1700s based on historical scholarship
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic commercial seaport — merchant trade, shipping, skilled crafts, and milling. Enslaved persons comprised a significant portion of the colonial workforce
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch (especially older families), English, French Huguenot, German, Sephardic Jewish, and West African (enslaved and free) communities were all present
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (dominant in early period), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, established 1697), Presbyterian, French Reformed (Huguenot), Lutheran, Quaker, and the first Jewish congregation (Shearith Israel, est. ca. 1654)
- **Key historical events:** Leisler's Rebellion (1689–1691); Queen Anne's War (1702–1713); French and Indian War (1754–1763); British occupation of New York City (1776–1783) during the American Revolution — many Loyalist families fled at war's end

---

## Boundary changes

- In the 1700s, New York City occupied the southern tip of Manhattan Island (New York County). The surrounding counties — Kings (Brooklyn), Queens, Richmond (Staten Island), and Westchester — were distinct jurisdictions with their own record series
- The five-borough consolidation did not occur until 1898; colonial-era records for Brooklyn, Queens, and Staten Island are held separately under Kings, Queens, and Richmond Counties
- New York Province records predate the State of New York (formed 1788) — researchers must consult both provincial archives and later state-level record series as a continuous trail

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil (government) registration of births, marriages, and deaths did **not** exist in colonial New York. The state did not begin civil registration until 1880. For the 1700s, **church records are the only systematic vital record source**
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers (see below); published abstracts; newspaper notices

### Church records
The most essential source class for this period. Per the FamilySearch Wiki article *New York City Genealogy*:

- **Dutch Reformed Church** — The oldest continuous register series, beginning 1639; the registers run through 1776 and beyond. FamilySearch has digitized **1 volume (imageGroupNumber 007733180) covering 1700–1776, containing 211 images**. ⚠️ **This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image. Records are in Dutch; researchers must read Dutch-language register entries**
- **Anglican / Church of England (Trinity Church)** — Founded 1697 at the corner of Broadway and Wall Street; baptism, marriage, and burial registers survive and have been published and indexed. Trinity Church Archives holds the originals; published transcriptions are widely available
- **Presbyterian** — First Presbyterian Church of New York (est. 1716); records survive
- **French Reformed (Huguenot)** — French-speaking Huguenot congregation; records survive from the late 1600s
- **Lutheran** — German-speaking Lutheran community records
- **Shearith Israel (Jewish)** — Congregation records survive from the colonial period

**FamilySearch Collection:** *New York, Church Records, 1640–1940* (collection ID 1469062) — approximately 2.3 million records/images at the state level, covering all denominations; date range overlaps the target window fully
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (digitized); New-York Historical Society; New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS); individual church archives; denominational repositories

### Census records
- **No federal census** before 1790 — the first U.S. Federal Census is outside the colonial period
- **Colonial enumerations:** New York Province conducted periodic censuses and musters; these survive in fragmentary form at the New York State Archives
- **Substitutes:** Tax assessment lists by ward (see Tax Records below); militia rolls (see Military Records)

### Probate and court records
Per the FamilySearch Wiki article *New York City Genealogy*:

- **Prerogative Court of New York** — Wills proved at the provincial level throughout the 1700s. The *Abstracts of Wills* series (published by the New-York Historical Society) indexes colonial wills; this is a critical finding aid
- **Mayor's Court** — New York City's colonial civil court; records survive and include property disputes, debt actions, and other civil matters useful for family reconstruction
- **FamilySearch Collection:** *New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971* (collection ID 1542780) — approximately 987,000 records/images; date range covers the entire colonial period

### Land records
- **System:** Metes-and-bounds (colonial grant/patent system under the Crown)
- **Types:** Land grants and patents from the colonial governor; deeds and conveyances; manorial leases (some large landholders held manorial patents)
- **FamilySearch Collection:** *New York, Land Records, 1630–1975* (collection ID 2078654) — approximately 1.6 million records/images; date range covers the full colonial period
- **New York State Archives** holds the original colonial land patents and grant records

### Military records
Per the FamilySearch Wiki article *New York City Genealogy*:

- **Colonial militia rolls** — New York Province maintained militia lists that enumerate men of military age by ward; useful for confirming residence and identifying families
- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702–1713); King George's War (1744–1748); French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolution (1775–1783)
- **Revolutionary War service:** Records held at the National Archives (NARA); New York State Archives holds state-level muster rolls. **Fold3.com** hosts digitized NARA military records (subscription)
- **Loyalist claims:** Many Loyalists filed compensation claims with the British government after 1783; these records survive at the UK National Archives (Kew) and are partially available online through Ancestry and LAC (Library and Archives Canada)

### Tax records
Per the FamilySearch Wiki article *New York City Genealogy*:

- **Colonial tax assessment lists** survive for some years and wards of New York City; these serve as a census substitute and can confirm a person's presence in a specific ward
- **Note:** *New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804* (collection ID 1678432) is the earliest FamilySearch-digitized tax collection, but its date range (1799–1804) falls **outside** the colonial target window. For 1700–1783 tax records, consult the New York State Archives and the New-York Historical Society

### Newspaper records
- **New York Gazette** (est. 1725, the first newspaper in New York) — marriage and death notices, legal notices, runaway servant/enslaved person advertisements, and ship arrivals
- **New York Weekly Journal** (est. 1733, John Peter Zenger)
- **Where held:** Early issues on microfilm at the New York Public Library (NYPL) and New York State Library; **Newspapers.com** and **Readex/America's Historical Newspapers** (subscription) hold digitized colonial newspaper runs
- **Research value:** Marriage and death notices; lists of merchants, ship passengers, and debtors; estate notices

### Immigration records
- New York was the primary Atlantic port of entry for the colonies. **No formal federal passenger list system existed until 1820**, so colonial-era arrivals are documented through:
  - Ship manifests in British colonial port records (fragmentary)
  - Naturalization records — the Denization and Naturalization Acts; surviving records at the New York State Archives
  - Customs/port records — some survive at the New York State Archives and NARA

### Cemetery records
- **Trinity Churchyard** (Manhattan) — one of the oldest surviving burying grounds in the U.S.; many colonial New Yorkers are buried here; records and transcriptions are widely available
- **Other colonial burying grounds:** Dutch Reformed (now Marble Cemetery area), Jewish (Chatham Square Cemetery, est. 1683, the oldest surviving Jewish cemetery in the U.S.)
- **FindAGrave.com** has coverage for Trinity and other historic NYC cemeteries; physical sexton records may be held by the churches

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |

| **FamilySearch** | *New York, Church Records, 1640–1940* (2.3M records); *New York, Land Records, 1630–1975* (1.6M records); *New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971* (987K records); 1 Dutch Reformed register volume (007733180, browse-only, in Dutch) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | New York colonial church records, land records, probate; Revolutionary War records | Subscription |

| **Newspapers.com / Readex** | New York Gazette and other colonial-era newspapers | Subscription |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Revolutionary War service and pension records | Free (NARA catalog) / Fold3 for images |

### Physical repositories
