| **New York State Archives** (Albany) | New York Colonial Manuscripts; provincial census fragments; land patents; militia rolls; colonial court records | In-person / some digitized |
| **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS)** | Church record transcriptions; vital records abstracts; colonial-era published indexes | Membership / in-person (NYC) |
| **New-York Historical Society** | *Abstracts of Wills* (colonial probate index); colonial newspapers; manuscript collections | In-person / some online |
| **New York Public Library (NYPL)** | Newspaper microfilm; map collections; colonial imprints | In-person / NYPL Digital Collections online |
| **Trinity Church Archives** | Trinity Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers from 1697 | By appointment |
| **Congregation Shearith Israel** | Earliest Jewish community records in North America | By appointment |

---

## Records NOT online

- **New York Colonial Manuscripts** (governor's papers, council minutes, provincial administration records) — held at the New York State Archives; calendared and partially published in the *Documents Relative to the Colonial History of the State of New York* (O'Callaghan, 15 vols.), but not fully digitized
- **Mayor's Court records** — physical only at the New York City Municipal Archives
- **Colonial tax assessment ward lists** (pre-1799) — physical/microfilm at New York State Archives and NYHS; not in FamilySearch's digitized collections
- **Colonial militia rolls** — available in published transcriptions and at the New York State Archives; not fully digitized online
- **French Reformed and Lutheran church registers** — partial microfilm at FamilySearch; consult the Family History Library catalog

---

## Known record losses

- No major courthouse fires comparable to other colonial cities; New York City records survived relatively well
- **British occupation (1776–1783):** Wartime disruption affected record-keeping; some church records have gaps during the occupation years. Trinity Church, used as a military depot, may have gaps. Dutch Reformed registers appear to stop at 1776 in the FamilySearch-digitized volume
- **Great Fire of 1776:** A major fire destroyed a large portion of lower Manhattan during the British occupation; some records and property were lost
- **Substitute sources for gaps:** Church vestry minutes; published abstracts (Abstracts of Wills, etc.); newspaper notices; colonial census enumerations; land conveyance records

---

## Research tips

1. **Church records are your vital records.** There was no civil registration in colonial New York. Start with the denomination of your ancestor — Dutch Reformed for Dutch families, Anglican for English, Presbyterian for Scots-Irish. The FamilySearch Wiki article *New York City Genealogy* identifies the Dutch Reformed registers as the oldest continuous series
2. **The Dutch Reformed register volume (007733180) is browse-only and in Dutch.** You must navigate image-by-image with no name index and read entries in Dutch; consider using a translation resource or the published English-language transcriptions of these registers
3. **Wills are heavily indexed.** The *Abstracts of Wills* (New-York Historical Society, covering 1665–1801) is a published, indexed series covering the Prerogative Court wills — consult this before searching unindexed original volumes
4. **Ward is the key geographic subdivision.** Colonial NYC was divided into wards (South, Dock, East, West, North, Montgomery, Out Ward). Many tax, militia, and church records are organized by ward — identify which ward your ancestor lived in to focus your search
5. **Check for Loyalist records.** If your family left NYC around 1783, they may appear in British Loyalist compensation claims, muster rolls of Loyalist regiments, or emigration records to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, or Ontario
6. **The five-borough consolidation is 1898.** For ancestors in Brooklyn (Kings County), Queens, or Staten Island (Richmond County) in the 1700s, research their records in those separate county jurisdictions — not New York City/New York County
7. **NYGBS and NYHS are essential.** The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society and the New-York Historical Society hold decades of published abstracts, indexes, and transcriptions of colonial records that make searching far more efficient than working from unindexed originals
8. **Newspaper notices substitute for missing vital records.** Marriage and death notices in the *New York Gazette* (from 1725) can document events not found in church registers

# Locality Guide: New York City, Colonial Period (1700–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **City established:** 1624/1626 as New Amsterdam (Dutch colony); seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York
- **Administrative center:** New York City (Manhattan/New York County), seat of New York Province under British colonial rule
- **Parent jurisdiction during period:** New York Province (British Crown colony), 1664–1783. State of New York not formed until 1788
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic commercial seaport — merchant trade, shipping, skilled crafts, milling; enslaved persons a significant portion of the colonial workforce
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch, English, French Huguenot, German, Sephardic Jewish, West African (enslaved and free)
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, est. 1697), Presbyterian, French Reformed (Huguenot), Lutheran, Quaker, Shearith Israel (Jewish, est. ca. 1654)
- **Key historical events:** Leisler's Rebellion (1689–1691); French and Indian War (1754–1763); British occupation 1776–1783; Great Fire of 1776

## Boundary changes
- In the 1700s NYC occupied southern Manhattan (New York County). Kings, Queens, Richmond, and Westchester were distinct jurisdictions
- Five-borough consolidation not until 1898 — colonial records for Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island held separately
- New York Province records predate State of New York (1788)

## Available record types

### Vital records
- No civil registration in colonial period; state registration began 1880. Church records are the sole systematic vital source.

### Church records
- **Dutch Reformed** — oldest continuous registers from 1639; FamilySearch has 1 volume (007733180), 211 images, 1700–1776. ⚠️ 0% indexed, not full-text searchable, browse-only, in Dutch
- **Anglican/Trinity Church** — founded 1697; baptism/marriage/burial registers published and indexed; Trinity Church Archives holds originals
- **Presbyterian** — First Presbyterian (est. 1716); records survive
- **French Reformed (Huguenot)** — records survive from late 1600s
- **Shearith Israel** — oldest Jewish community records in North America
- FamilySearch Collection 1469062: New York, Church Records, 1640–1940 (~2.3M records)

### Census records
- No federal census before 1790. Colonial enumerations survive fragmentarily at New York State Archives.
- Substitutes: tax assessment lists by ward; militia rolls

### Probate and court records
- Prerogative Court of New York wills indexed in *Abstracts of Wills* (NYHS, 1665–1801)
- Mayor's Court records survive; physical only at NYC Municipal Archives
- FamilySearch Collection 1542780: New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971 (~987K records)

### Land records
- Colonial grant/patent system; deeds and conveyances
- FamilySearch Collection 2078654: New York, Land Records, 1630–1975 (~1.6M records)
- New York State Archives holds original colonial land patents

### Military records
- Colonial militia rolls survive; useful for ward residence
- Revolutionary War service at NARA; Fold3 has digitized NARA military records
- Loyalist claims at UK National Archives (Kew)

### Tax records
- Colonial ward tax assessment lists survive (some years) — not digitized on FamilySearch; at New York State Archives and NYHS
- FamilySearch Collection 1678432 (Tax Assessment Rolls 1799–1804) falls outside the colonial window

### Newspaper records
- *New York Gazette* (est. 1725); *New York Weekly Journal* (est. 1733)
- Newspapers.com / Readex America's Historical Newspapers (subscription)
- Microfilm at NYPL and New York State Library

### Immigration records
- No formal federal passenger lists until 1820; colonial arrivals documented through British port records, denization/naturalization records at New York State Archives

### Cemetery records
- Trinity Churchyard (Anglican); Chatham Square Cemetery (Jewish, est. 1683, oldest surviving Jewish cemetery in U.S.)
- FindAGrave has coverage for historic NYC cemeteries

- Substitutes: church vestry minutes; published abstracts; newspaper notices; land conveyance records

# Virginia — Revolutionary War Era (1775–1783)
### Locality Research Guide: Military Service & Wartime Family Records

---

## Jurisdictional Context

**Virginia, United States** (standardPlace; a state from 1788, but operating as a self-governing Commonwealth from 1776). Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies and contributed more Continental Army soldiers than any other colony/state. County-level record-keeping dates from the 1630s, making Virginia one of the best-documented pre-federal jurisdictions. All civil records during 1775–1783 were created at the **county courthouse** level; no statewide civil registration existed. The 1790 federal census for Virginia was **destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814 — this is the single most important structural gap for this period (see Quirks).

---

## Primary Record Classes for Military & Wartime Research

### 1. 🎖️ Military Service Records *(FamilySearch — indexed)*
**FamilySearch Collection:** *Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783* (collection ID 1945678)
- Exact date match to your target window
- Covers Continental Line and state militia service
- Accessible at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678

Per the FamilySearch Wiki article *[Virginia Military Records — Revolutionary War]*:
- **Continental Line muster rolls and service records** are held at the **National Archives (NARA), Record Group 93**. These document enlistments, pay, and discharges for men serving in the Continental Army.
- **Virginia militia records** are held at the **Library of Virginia, Richmond**. Militia service was county-organized and frequently documented at the local court level as well.
- **Virginia State Navy records** have been published and are available through the Library of Virginia and in print finding aids.

**How to access NARA RG 93:** Request through the National Archives catalog (catalog.archives.gov) or order compiled service record abstracts through Fold3.com (see External Repositories below).

---

### 2. 💰 Pension & Bounty Land Warrant Records *(NARA — largely digitized)*
These are among the richest genealogical sources for the Revolution nationwide. Per the wiki article *[Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands]*:

- **Pension and Bounty-Land Warrant Application Files** — **NARA Record Group 15**. Applications submitted after the war often contain detailed personal narratives, family information, widow's declarations, and sworn depositions by neighbors — far more biographical detail than service records alone.
- **Virginia Military District of Ohio bounty-land warrants** — Virginia granted land in what is now Ohio to its veterans. Warrant and survey records at the **Virginia State Library** connect veterans to those Ohio land claims.
- Fold3.com has extensively digitized these pension files; the **Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR)** has also compiled pension abstracts for Virginia patriots.

---

### 3. 📋 Tax Records — *Substitute for the Missing 1790 Census* *(FamilySearch — indexed)*
**FamilySearch Collection:** *Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850* (collection ID 1456723)
- Begins 1782 — partially overlaps the war's final years
- Accessible at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723

> ⚠️ **Critical quirk:** Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed in the 1814 burning of Washington. **County personal property tax lists from 1782–1790** are the standard substitute. These lists name heads of household and enumerate taxable property, functioning as a near-census for locating families in the immediate post-war period. This is the first place to look for a family's whereabouts in Revolutionary-era Virginia.

Per the FamilySearch Wiki: *"County tax lists from the 1780s are among the earliest substitutes for the missing 1790 Virginia federal census."*

---

### 4. 📜 Land, Marriage & Will Records *(FamilySearch — indexed)*
**FamilySearch Collection:** *Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900* (collection ID 1734285)
- Full coverage of the target period
- Accessible at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285

Wartime land records are particularly valuable because:
- **Deed books** capture property transactions — soldiers selling land before departure, widows selling estates after death
- **Wills and estate inventories** from 1775–1783 may name soldiers who died in service or document who administered the estates of fallen soldiers
- **Marriage bonds** establish family connections for both soldiers and their families

---

### 5. ⛪ Church Records *(FamilySearch — indexed)*
**FamilySearch Collection:** *Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929* (collection ID 1598230)
- Full coverage of the target period
- Accessible at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230

The **Anglican (later Episcopal) vestry book** was the primary civil–religious record-keeping mechanism in colonial and Revolutionary-era Virginia. Vestry books recorded:
- Births, baptisms, marriages, and burials
- Poor relief recipients (including soldiers' destitute families)
- Land processioning (boundary walks confirming property lines)

Other denominations active in 1775–1783 Virginia include Presbyterian, Baptist, Methodist, and Quaker congregations — each with separate registers. Check both FamilySearch and the respective denominational archives.

---

### 6. 🏛️ County Court Records *(FamilySearch — indexed)*
**FamilySearch Collection:** *Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920* (collection ID 2134567)
- Full coverage of the target period
- Accessible at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567

Virginia's county courts were the center of civil life during the Revolution. Wartime-relevant filings include:
- **Guardianship records** for orphaned children of soldiers killed in service
- **Loyalist/Tory proceedings** — confiscation of Loyalist property was adjudicated at the county level
- **Oaths of allegiance** to the Commonwealth
- **Ordinary (tavern) licenses** — useful for tracing the community networks around military encampments
- **Court order books** — name witnesses, jurors, bondsmen, and administrators who can corroborate family connections

> ⚠️ **"Burned counties" caveat:** Many Virginia county courthouses burned during the Civil War (1861–1865), creating gaps in county-level records. When county records are absent for the 1775–1783 period, check the Library of Virginia for any copied or abstracted records, and consult the parent county (Virginia frequently subdivided counties across this era).

## Research Quirks & Gotchas

1. **Missing 1790 census:** Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed. Use 1782–1790 county personal property tax lists (in the Tax Records 1782–1850 collection) as your primary substitute for locating families in this period.

2. **Burned county courthouses:** Dozens of Virginia county courthouses were destroyed in the Civil War. When county records are missing, check the Library of Virginia for pre-war copies, abstracts, or microfilm made before the destruction.

3. **Virginia Military District of Ohio:** Veterans who received bounty land often appear in Ohio land records, not just Virginia. Search warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library to connect a Virginia soldier to an Ohio land claim.

4. **County subdivisions:** Virginia actively subdivided counties throughout the late 18th century. Your ancestor's county of residence in 1775 may have become a different county by 1783. Always check which county held jurisdiction over a specific location in a specific year before declaring records absent.

5. **FamilySearch wiki coverage:** The FamilySearch Wiki place-pages for Virginia returned only generic content in this search. For Virginia-specific guidance, consult the FamilySearch Wiki article *[Virginia Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records)* directly, which provides detailed guidance on NARA record groups and published sources.

6. **Pension files contain family narrative:** Don't stop at service records. Widow's pension applications (filed decades after the war) often contain the richest family detail — names of children, marriage dates, land descriptions, and neighbor witnesses who corroborate the soldier's service.

---

## Suggested Research Path

1. **Start at FamilySearch** — search the *Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783* collection (ID 1945678) for the soldier by name.
2. **Check pension files on Fold3** — search NARA RG 15 pension and bounty-land warrant applications; include widow's applications filed in the soldier's name.
3. **Pull the 1782–1790 tax lists** from the *Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850* collection to place the family in a specific county before and after the war.
4. **Search county court records** for guardianships, oaths of allegiance, and estate proceedings at the county where the family lived.
5. **Check land and will records** for wartime deeds and post-war estate settlements that name heirs.
6. **Contact the Library of Virginia** for militia records and any county records not yet fully digitized.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (Early 1800s — c. 1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** City founded 1718 by France; ceded to Spain 1763; retroceded to France 1800; transferred to the United States via the **Louisiana Purchase, 1803**; organized as the **Territory of Orleans 1804**; admitted as the **State of Louisiana, 18 April 1812**
- **Administrative unit:** Orleans **Parish** — Louisiana uses the parish system (not counties), inherited from Spanish and French colonial administration
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans itself served as the seat of Orleans Parish and capital of the Territory/State of Louisiana through much of this period
- **Legal tradition:** **Civil law (Napoleonic Code)**, not English common law. This fundamentally shapes what records were created: Louisiana has *successions* (not probate), *tutorships* (not guardianships), *interdictions* (incompetency), and notarized acts for virtually every legal transaction. Researchers accustomed to common-law states will need to reframe their expectations entirely.
- **Population:** Population data was not returned by the place tool for this fixture; census records themselves (see below) are the best population indicator.
- **Economy:** Major port city; cotton and sugar trade; enslaved labor; shipping, banking, and commerce; free people of color community unique in North America
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, African (enslaved and free), Anglo-American (increasing after 1803), German, Irish, Caribbean (especially Saint-Domingue refugees after 1809)
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral the dominant institution); Methodist, Presbyterian, and Protestant congregations growing after 1803
- **Key historical events affecting records:** Great Fire of 1788 (destroyed ~856 buildings); Second Great Fire of 1794 (destroyed ~212 more buildings); Louisiana Purchase 1803; Battle of New Orleans 1815 (War of 1812); repeated yellow fever epidemics; periodic Mississippi River floods

---

## Boundary and jurisdictional changes

New Orleans sits at the intersection of **three successive colonial regimes** during the early 1800s, each of which created records in a different language and under different legal authority:

| Period | Governing authority | Record language(s) | Legal system |
|---|---|---|---|
| To 1763 | French Crown | French | French civil law |
| 1763–1803 | Spanish Crown (Cabildo) | Spanish, French | Spanish/French civil law |
| 1803–1812 | U.S. Territory of Orleans | French, English | Transitional — civil law retained |
| 1812 onward | State of Louisiana | English, French | Louisiana civil law |

**Critical implication:** Records for the same family may shift language mid-sequence. Church records at St. Louis Cathedral ran continuously through all regime changes, but the governing authority that created civil records changed at each transition. When searching for an ancestor in the early 1800s, you may need to search records created under Spanish authority (pre-1803) to find the family's earlier history.

---

## Disaster history and what survived

### The Great Fires of 1788 and 1794
The **Good Friday Fire of 21 March 1788** destroyed approximately 856 buildings and an unknown quantity of government and church records from the French colonial period. The **Second Great Fire of 8 December 1794** destroyed approximately 212 additional buildings. Both fires swept through the French Quarter (Vieux Carré), which was the administrative and religious center of colonial New Orleans.

**What was lost:** A significant portion of pre-1788 civil and notarial records. The losses are not fully catalogued.

**What survived despite the fires** (per the FamilySearch Wiki article *New Orleans Genealogy*, section "Records Surviving Disasters"):
> "Significant genealogical sources survive for the early 1800s: sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, though with gaps), notarial records, and the records of the Cabildo (Spanish colonial governing body). The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734."

The fires destroyed *buildings* but copies, duplicates, and off-site records allowed significant survival. The notarial system required acts to be recorded in bound registers held by individual notaries — surviving registers from notaries who were not burned out have come down largely intact.

### Ongoing flood and storm risk
New Orleans sits below sea level and suffered recurring floods from the Mississippi River and Gulf storms throughout the 1800s. These affected physical repositories unevenly — the most significant archival losses in the 19th century were from fire, not flood, but researchers should be aware that some local holdings (church basements, civic offices) sustained water damage.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Louisiana did **not** have statewide civil registration of births and deaths until **1914**. Marriage registration in Orleans Parish began earlier (parish-level civil marriage bonds/licenses survive from the territorial period), but coverage is inconsistent before the 1830s.
- **Early 1800s vital records:** **Do not exist as a civil registration system.** Church sacramental registers are the primary (often only) source for births, marriages, and deaths.
- **FamilySearch collection overlapping period:** The **Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964** (collection 1543892) begins in 1819 and is fully indexed (2,345,678 records) but has **no images** — it is an index only. Treat it as a finding aid pointing to underlying records.
- **Access — Death Index:** Indexed + images online (index only; no image attached) | Free at FamilySearch

### Church records ⭐ *Primary substitute for all civil vital records*
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic — St. Louis Cathedral is the anchor institution. Protestant congregations (Methodist, Presbyterian) began forming after 1803 but their early registers are sparse.
- **St. Louis Cathedral records:** Sacramental registers of baptisms, marriages, and burials survive **from 1731**, with gaps caused by the 1788 and 1794 fires. The registers that survived cover the early 1800s with reasonable continuity. They are in **French** (and sometimes Spanish or Latin) for the territorial period.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925** (collection 1612905) — 987,654 records with 493,827 images. **Indexed + images**; searchable by name online. This is your first stop for any vital event in early New Orleans.
- **Language warning:** Records from c. 1800–1815 may be in French, Spanish, or a mixture. The researcher must be prepared to read the original-language entries; index transcriptions can misrender French and Spanish names.
- **Access:** Indexed + images | Free at FamilySearch (collection 1612905)
- **Originals held:** Archives of the Archdiocese of New Orleans; St. Louis Cathedral archives

### Notarial records ⭐ *The backbone of Louisiana legal documentation — no equivalent in other U.S. states*
- **What they are:** Under Louisiana's civil law system, notaries public authenticated and recorded virtually every significant legal transaction: sales (of property, enslaved persons, businesses), successions (wills and intestate estates), marriage contracts, emancipations, apprenticeships, debt acknowledgments, and more. They substitute for, and go far beyond, what deeds and probate records capture in common-law states.
- **Survival:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds **over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734** (per FamilySearch Wiki). This is one of the largest surviving notarial archives in the Western Hemisphere. The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed some registers but a substantial corpus survived.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group **004990115** — *Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies)*, Orleans, Louisiana, **1803–1820** — 167 images, in **French and English**.
  - ⚠️ **Browse-only:** 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image.
  - ⚠️ **Language:** French and English. French predominates for the early years.
- **Primary repository:** **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**, 1340 Poydras Street, New Orleans, LA 70112. Holds the full run of surviving acts; their own finding aids and index are far more complete than the FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Access — FamilySearch volume:** Browse-only images | Free at FamilySearch (image group 004990115)
- **Access — Full holdings:** Physical/in-person at the Notarial Archives Research Center (online search tool available at notarialarchives.org)

### Census records
- **Federal census years overlapping the period:** 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840 (and 1800 for the Territory of Orleans predecessor jurisdiction; 1850 slightly postdates the early 1800s but captures families established in the period).
  - **1800:** Orleans Territory — population enumerated under the territorial structure
  - **1810:** First full Louisiana state census after statehood
  - **1820, 1830, 1840:** Standard federal censuses; New Orleans grows dramatically
  - **Note:** The **1890 federal census was largely destroyed by fire** in Washington, D.C. (1921) — not relevant to the early 1800s period, but important context for later research
- **Enslaved persons:** Pre-1870 federal censuses list enslaved people only as numbers (not by name) in separate slave schedules. Enslaved individuals are identified by name in notarial acts (sales, emancipations), church baptismal records, and estate inventories.
- **Access:** Ancestry.com (subscription) — U.S. Federal Census Collection; also FamilySearch (free)

### Probate and succession records ⭐ *Uniquely rich in Louisiana*
- **Louisiana term:** "Successions" (not probate). Under civil law, successions include wills, intestate administrations, estate inventories, and tutorship appointments for minor heirs. They routinely name all heirs, their relationship to the deceased, and may include detailed property inventories.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984** (collection 2078341) — 456,789 records with 228,394 images. **Indexed + images**; covers the full early 1800s period.
- **Notarial component:** Many succession acts are embedded in notarial registers rather than filed separately at a courthouse. Search both the Probate Records collection and the notarial archives.
- **Access:** Indexed + images | Free at FamilySearch (collection 2078341)
- **Physical originals:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court records; Louisiana State Archives

### Land records
- **System:** Louisiana is a **federal land state** for land granted after the Louisiana Purchase (1803). Pre-1803 grants follow French and Spanish colonial land law (arpents, not acres; long-lot system along the Mississippi River). Colonial-era grants were confirmed or contested by the U.S. Board of Land Commissioners after 1803.
- **Types relevant to the period:** French and Spanish land grants (pre-1803); U.S. federal land patents (post-1803); notarial acts of sale (the primary record of private land transfer throughout the period — see Notarial records above); mortgage acts; tax records.
- **Federal patents:** Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (GLO) — glorecords.blm.gov — free online
- **Colonial grants:** Louisiana State Land Office; Louisiana State Archives
- **Private sales:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (acts of sale)
- **Access:** BLM GLO patents online free; notarial acts browse-only at FamilySearch or physical at Notarial Archives

### Military records
- **War of 1812 / Battle of New Orleans (8 January 1815):** New Orleans is the site of the war's most famous American victory. Service records, muster rolls, and pension files for Louisiana militia and U.S. regulars who fought here are held at NARA. Louisiana's multiracial free colored militia ("Battalion of Free Men of Color") also served and left records.
- **Territorial militia:** Earlier militia records from the territorial period (post-1803) exist at the Louisiana State Archives and NARA.
- **Access:** Service records and pensions — NARA (fold3.com subscription; Ancestry.com); Louisiana State Archives for state militia records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** New Orleans has distinctive above-ground tomb cemeteries: St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (est. 1823), and others. High mortality from yellow fever epidemics means burial records are voluminous.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave.com indexes many New Orleans cemetery inscriptions.
- **Sexton records:** Burial records for Catholic cemeteries are held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans and some are included in the FamilySearch church records collection.
- **Access:** FindAGrave (free online); physical sexton records at Archdiocese archives

### Newspaper records
- **Early papers:** *Le Moniteur de la Louisiane* (founded 1794 — the first newspaper in Louisiana, in French); *Louisiana Gazette* (English, founded 1804 after the Purchase); *L'Ami des Lois*. New Orleans had a vibrant bilingual press from the early territorial period.
- **Value:** Obituaries, marriage announcements, legal notices (succession ads, sheriff's sales), ship passenger arrivals, runaway enslaved person notices (a crucial substitute source for tracing enslaved individuals).
- **Online access:** Newspapers.com (subscription); Louisiana Digital Library (some free); Library of Congress Chronicling America (some issues)
- **Physical holdings:** New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Division; Tulane University Howard-Tilton Memorial Library

### Immigration records
- **Port of New Orleans** was a major point of entry, second only to New York for much of the 19th century. Passenger arrival lists begin with meaningful coverage around 1820.
- **FamilySearch / Ancestry:** U.S. passenger lists indexed and available online for post-1820 arrivals; earlier arrivals may appear in notarial records (contracts, bond acts) or Spanish/French colonial entry records.
- **Saint-Domingue refugees:** A large wave of refugees from the Haitian Revolution (esp. 1809–1810) brought thousands of French-speaking free people of color and enslaved persons to New Orleans — a distinct community with its own records trail.
- **Access:** Ancestry.com (subscription) for federal passenger lists; NARA for originals

### Tax records
- **Substitute value:** Louisiana territorial and state tax lists (assessments) can partially substitute for missing census years and document property ownership.
- **Held at:** Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge); some records at the New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Division
- **Access:** Physical/in-person at repositories; limited digitization

### Enslaved persons records — a critical specialized category
New Orleans was a major hub of the internal slave trade. Researchers tracing enslaved ancestors in early New Orleans should consult:
1. **Notarial acts of sale** — name the person sold, sometimes age and origin
2. **Manumission acts** (also notarial) — document emancipations
3. **Baptismal registers** at St. Louis Cathedral — enslaved persons were baptized; entries often include owner's name and sometimes African origin or parentage
4. **Estate inventories** within succession records — list enslaved persons by name and value
5. **Runaway notices** in newspapers

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (col. 1612905); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (col. 2078341); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (col. 1543892); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (col. 1798054); Notarial Acts browse volume 004990115 (1803–1820) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1800–1850); U.S. passenger lists; some Louisiana collections | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military records, War of 1812 | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | New Orleans cemetery inscriptions | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical Louisiana newspapers | Subscription |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Federal records, War of 1812 service/pension files, federal land patents, passenger lists | Free / in-person |
| **BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov)** | Federal land patents post-1803 | Free |
| **notarialarchives.org** | New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center finding aids | Free search; originals in-person |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**, 1340 Poydras St., New Orleans | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734; all surviving registers | In-person; online index |
| **Louisiana State Archives**, Baton Rouge | Territorial and early state records; land records; militia records | In-person; some online |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** | Church sacramental registers (baptism, marriage, burial); cemetery records | In-person / correspondence |
| **New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division** | City directories; newspapers; municipal records | In-person |
| **Historic New Orleans Collection** | Manuscripts, photographs, maps, colonial records | In-person |
| **Tulane University, Howard-Tilton Memorial Library** | Louisiana history collections; newspapers; manuscripts | In-person |
| **Orleans Parish Civil District Court** | Succession (probate) records; court filings | In-person |

---

## Records NOT online

The following records exist but are **not fully available in any online database** — their absence from online searches does not mean they do not exist:

- **Full run of New Orleans notarial acts** — only a small slice (167 images, 1803–1820, browse-only) is on FamilySearch; the complete 30+ million pages are at the Notarial Archives Research Center
- **Spanish Cabildo records** (pre-1803 colonial governing body) — partially held at the Louisiana State Museum / Cabildo building; not digitized
- **Pre-1820 city directory records** (partial survival)
- **Orleans Parish civil court records** not captured in the FamilySearch probate collection
- **Early territorial tax lists** — not digitized
- **Most pre-1820 newspaper runs** — partial digitization only
- **Archdiocese baptismal/marriage/burial registers** not yet captured in the FS church records collection

---

## Known record losses

| Loss event | Date | What was lost | Substitute sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Great Fire (Good Friday Fire)** | 21 March 1788 | ~856 buildings destroyed; significant pre-1788 French colonial civil and notarial records lost | Surviving notarial registers from unburned offices; duplicate/copy records; St. Louis Cathedral registers (partial survival) |
| **Second Great Fire** | 8 December 1794 | Additional ~212 buildings; further archival losses | Same substitutes as above; Spanish colonial records that were held off-site |
| **Ongoing flood/storm damage** | Throughout 19th c. | Sporadic damage to local repositories; not a single catastrophic event | Off-site copies; Archdiocese archives; Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge, away from flood zone) |
| **1890 U.S. Census fire** | 1921 (Washington, D.C.) | Most of the 1890 federal census destroyed nationally | 1880 + 1900 censuses bracket the gap; city directories; tax records; state enumerations |

**Bottom line on disaster survival:** The fires of 1788 and 1794 are serious losses but they are *pre-period* for most early-1800s research. A family arriving or living in New Orleans in 1800–1850 is well-documented **if** you know where to look. The St. Louis Cathedral registers survived with gaps, the notarial archives survived robustly, and FamilySearch has digitized key collections. The main challenge is not destruction — it is access (browse-only volumes, French-language records, physical-only repositories) and the unfamiliarity of Louisiana's civil-law record types to researchers trained on common-law states.

---

## Research tips

1. **Search church records first, not civil registration.** There was no Louisiana civil registration of births or deaths until 1914. The **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925** collection (FamilySearch, indexed + images, collection 1612905) is your primary source for vital events throughout the entire early 1800s.

2. **Think "successions," not "probate."** The **Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984** collection (FamilySearch, indexed + images, collection 2078341) uses Louisiana civil-law terminology. Successions routinely name all heirs with their relationship to the deceased — an invaluable tool when vital records are thin.

3. **The notarial archives are irreplaceable.** For any ancestor with property, business dealings, or legal transactions in New Orleans before 1850, the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (notarialarchives.org) holds records that exist nowhere else. Plan for an in-person visit or a paid research query if you cannot travel.

4. **Read the language.** Records from c. 1800–1815 are frequently in French (and sometimes Spanish). Index transcriptions can misrender Creole and French names. When a search yields nothing, try variant spellings or browse the original-language images directly.

5. **The FamilySearch notarial volume is browse-only.** Image group 004990115 (Notarial Acts, 1803–1820, Orleans) is 167 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable. To find a specific person in this volume, you must either browse every image or use the Notarial Archives' own finding aids to identify the relevant notary and date range first.

6. **Orleans Parish ≠ Orleans County.** Louisiana uses parishes, not counties. Always search under **Orleans Parish** in databases that use county-field searches; entering "Orleans County" will return nothing.

7. **Use the succession ads in newspapers as a finding aid.** Under Louisiana law, succession proceedings required public notice. Newspaper legal notices — published in both English and French papers — named deceased persons and their heirs, sometimes with addresses and relationships. *Le Moniteur de la Louisiane* (French) and the *Louisiana Gazette* (English) both covered the early 1800s.

8. **For enslaved ancestors, notarial acts and baptismal registers are essential.** Notarial acts of sale, manumission, and hiring out name enslaved individuals. St. Louis Cathedral baptismal registers recorded enslaved baptisms with owner's name, and sometimes the person's African nation or parentage. These are among the most detailed pre-emancipation records for enslaved people in North America.

9. **War of 1812 / Battle of New Orleans generates a separate record set.** If an ancestor was in New Orleans around 1815, check NARA for militia service records (including the Battalion of Free Men of Color) and pension files. Fold3 and Ancestry.com index these.

10. **Territorial censuses and tax lists fill the intercensal gaps.** The 1810 Territory of Orleans census and later state and city enumerations, combined with annual tax assessment lists at the Louisiana State Archives, can help locate a family between federal census years.

---

*Sources: FamilySearch collections search (Louisiana, 4 collections returned); FamilySearch volume search (Orleans, Louisiana, 1795–1850, 1 volume returned: image group 004990115); FamilySearch Wiki search, article "New Orleans Genealogy," section "Records Surviving Disasters"; Wikipedia article on New Orleans. The wiki_place_page tool returned only generic fallback content for Louisiana — specific FamilySearch Louisiana wiki guidance should be consulted directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy.*

---

To summarize the disaster-survival picture directly: **the 1788 and 1794 fires are the dominant record losses, but they struck before 1800.** For your early-1800s research window, the most important thing to know is that **St. Louis Cathedral registers and the notarial archives survived** those fires in substantial form — and together they cover what civil registration and deed/probate records cover in other states. The real gaps aren't from destruction; they're from records that were never fully digitized or indexed, particularly the vast notarial holdings, and from the language barrier in French- and Spanish-language documents. Start with the indexed FamilySearch church records collection, then plan a notarial archives visit or query for anything involving property or legal events.

## Locality Research Guide: Port of Boston Immigration, 1840s
**Place:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
**Period of focus:** 1840–1860
**Scope:** Tracing immigrants who arrived through the Port of Boston

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Boston was established in 1630 within Suffolk County (formed 1643), Massachusetts (statehood 1788). In the 1840s it was one of the five principal US ports of entry. The decade is dominated by the Irish Famine migration (1845–1852); by 1850 more than a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born. This wave also included German, English, and Canadian immigrants. Because **Massachusetts began statewide civil vital registration in 1841**, the 1840s sits at a transition point — some arrivals can be found in early civil records, but church registers and town records remain essential supplements.

---

### Record Classes and Where to Find Them

---

#### 1. 🚢 Customs Passenger Lists — *Primary Source*

**What they record:** 1840s lists (pre-1893 Steerage Act) typically capture name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin only — no parish, village, or next-of-kin. Manage expectations accordingly.

| Collection | Access | Details |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891** (FS Collection 1784312) | **Indexed + images** | 1,234,567 records on FamilySearch; covers the full Port of Boston run |
| **Digitized volume — Port of Boston, 1840–1850** (image group 003345210) | **Full-text searchable; 3% name-indexed** | 389 images; nearly all must be browsed image-by-image — search by full-text where possible |
| **Ancestry.com** | Indexed | Mirrors the same NARA RG 36 series; useful for cross-checking |

**Physical originals:** National Archives Record Group 36 (Customs Passenger Lists). Held at the **National Archives at Boston, Waltham, MA**.

> ⚠️ **Browse-first warning:** The specific 1840–1850 Boston volume (image group 003345210) is only 3% name-indexed on FamilySearch. Full-text search works, but if a name is unusual or handwriting is poor, plan to browse it page by page. The indexed FS collection (1784312) is the better starting point.

---

#### 2. 📰 The Boston Pilot "Missing Persons" Advertisements

An extraordinary Boston-specific resource. The *Pilot*, the Irish Catholic newspaper, published a running column (1831–1921) in which immigrants placed notices seeking lost relatives — recording townland, county of origin, and last known location. Now indexed as the **"Missing Persons" database** at **infowanted.bc.edu** (Boston College). Invaluable when a passenger list gives only "Ireland" as origin.

---

#### 3. ✝️ Church Records — *Essential for 1840s Irish Immigrants*

Civil registration had just started; many families relied on parish baptisms, marriages, and burial entries as their only vital records.

| Collection | Access |
|---|---|
| **Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920** (FS Collection 1921657) | **Indexed + images**, 987,654 records |
| Catholic parishes (Cathedral of the Holy Cross; St. Patrick's, Lowell Rd) | **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** — contact for access |

Per the FamilySearch wiki on *Massachusetts Church Records*, the Archdiocese of Boston Archives holds the original Catholic parish registers for the 1840s immigrant congregations.

---

#### 4. 📋 Civil Vital Records

Massachusetts statewide registration began 1841 — so birth, marriage, and death records exist for the full decade, though early compliance was uneven.

| Collection | Access |
|---|---|
| **Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890** (FS Collection 2061550) | **Indexed + images**, 3,456,789 records |

Also held at the **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) and the **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)**, which has an extensive Massachusetts vital records database.

---

#### 5. 🏛️ Naturalization Records — *Critical Follow-On Search*

Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in **any court of record** — federal, state, or local. For Boston arrivals, check:
- Suffolk County Superior Court
- US Circuit and District Courts for Massachusetts
- Municipal Court of Boston

| Collection | Access |
|---|---|
| **Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906** (FS Collection 1459213) | **Indexed + images**, 345,678 records |

**National Archives at Boston (Waltham)** holds federal court naturalization records. NARA's *Index to New England Naturalization Petitions, 1791–1906* (M1299) is a useful finding aid.

---

#### 6. 🗳️ Federal and State Census Records

| Census | Notes |
|---|---|
| 1840 federal census | Names head of household only; other household members appear as tick-marks by age/sex bracket |
| 1850 federal census | **First census to name every person**; includes birthplace — crucial for confirming immigrant origin country |
| 1850 mortality schedule | Records deaths in the year preceding the census date |
| Massachusetts state censuses | Various years; fill intercensal gaps |

---

#### 7. 📖 City Directories and Other Local Records

Boston city directories survive from the 1840s and are held at the **Boston Public Library**. They list heads of household by name and address/occupation — often the fastest way to pin down a neighborhood before searching vital or church records. Also consider:

- **Boston Board of Health death records** (Massachusetts Archives)
- **Almshouse / Poorhouse admission records** — many newly arrived Famine immigrants passed through these institutions; held at Massachusetts Archives
- **Suffolk County Probate Records, 1635–1991** (FS Collection 1678901, 567,890 records, indexed + images) — useful once a settler died or had property

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)** | NARA RG 36 customs passenger lists; federal court naturalizations |
| **Massachusetts Archives (Boston)** | Civil vital records, state census, almshouse records, court files |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** | Catholic parish baptism, marriage, and burial registers |
| **Boston Public Library** | City directories, *Boston Pilot* newspaper runs |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** | Massachusetts vital records, compiled genealogies, Irish research guides |
| **FamilySearch (online)** | Collections 1784312, 2061550, 1921657, 1459213, 1678901 |
| **Ancestry.com** | Passenger lists, federal census, city directories |

---

### Research Tips for 1840s Boston Immigrants

1. **Start with the indexed passenger list collection (FS 1784312) before browsing the raw volume.** The indexed collection will surface most arrivals faster; fall back to browse-only volume 003345210 if the indexed search returns nothing.
2. **1840s lists name only country of origin — usually "Ireland" or "Germany."** To get a specific townland or village, pivot to the *Pilot* "Missing Persons" database, Catholic parish registers (which may record exact Irish origin), or later naturalization declarations.
3. **The 1850 census is your anchor.** It names every person and records birthplace. Work backward from it to the passenger list, then forward to naturalization papers.
4. **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered.** Search the FamilySearch collection, but also check the specific court indexes at NARA Waltham and the Suffolk County courthouse.
5. **Complement with NEHGS.** The New England Historic Genealogical Society holds Massachusetts-specific compiled databases and published guides for Irish-American research that are not duplicated on FamilySearch.

---

### Coverage Gaps

- Population data for Boston in this period was not returned by the FamilySearch place tool; consult NEHGS or the Massachusetts Archives for demographic context.
- The specific Port of Boston 1840–1850 digitized volume (image group 003345210) is **only 3% name-indexed** — the bulk requires browse-image-by-image review.
- The FamilySearch wiki place pages for Massachusetts did not return place-specific content in this session; consult **[familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration)** directly for the most current guidance on this state's records.

# Locality Guide: Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma), 1830–1890

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Status during period:** Indian Territory — a federally designated territory, not an organized U.S. territory with standard civil government. The federal government held treaty authority; sovereign tribal governments (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek/Muscogee, and Seminole — the Five Civilized Tribes — plus Plains tribes in western portions) administered internal affairs through their own courts, councils, and record systems.
- **Administrative center:** No single capital; tribal capitals included Tahlequah (Cherokee), Tishomingo (Chickasaw), Doaksville/Tuskahoma (Choctaw), Okmulgee (Creek), and Wewoka (Seminole). Federal oversight was exercised through the Union Agency at Muskogee.
- **Oklahoma statehood:** 1907 — *no Oklahoma state records exist during the mid-1800s target period.*
- **Population:** The place_population tool returned no data for Indian Territory. Tribal populations during this period were recorded through annuity rolls and federal census special schedules, not standard U.S. census infrastructure.
- **Key context:** The Indian Removal Act of 1830 forced relocation of the Five Civilized Tribes from the southeastern United States to Indian Territory via the Trail of Tears. Federal treaty obligations created a substantial paper trail of annuity rolls, removal census records, and land agreements that are among the richest genealogical sources for this period.

---

## Boundary and jurisdictional changes

- Indian Territory as a defined region dates from approximately 1830 (Indian Removal Act). Its boundaries shifted as Congress reorganized the region.
- In 1890, the western half of Indian Territory was reorganized as **Oklahoma Territory** (the "Unassigned Lands" opened to non-Indian settlement). For families in western Oklahoma after 1890, records may be filed under Oklahoma Territory, not Indian Territory.
- Indian Territory and Oklahoma Territory merged at Oklahoma statehood in 1907.
- **Research implication:** Records created before 1890 are almost exclusively federal (BIA/NARA), tribal, or missionary. After 1890, two parallel jurisdictions existed side by side — check both Indian Territory *and* Oklahoma Territory records depending on where in present-day Oklahoma the family lived.

---

## Available record types

### Tribal enrollment rolls (the core record class)

This is the most important category for mid-1800s research.

**FamilySearch indexed collection:**
- **Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959** (Collection ID 1987432) — 567,890 records with 283,945 images. Date range 1851–1959 overlaps the target window directly. Access: [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432).

**FamilySearch digitized volume (browse + search):**
- Image group **002298871** — 940 images of **Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870**, covering Indian Territory. This volume is **99% name-indexed** and **full-text searchable** — the highest accessibility level. Search directly by name on FamilySearch.

**Named rolls within the target period (from the FamilySearch Wiki article "Oklahoma Native American Records"):**
- **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** — lists Cherokee who moved to Indian Territory before the main Removal.
- **Drennen Roll (1852)** — an early enumeration of Cherokee in Indian Territory.
- Both are indexed online at FamilySearch and Ancestry.

**Important note on the Dawes Rolls:** The FamilySearch Wiki notes that the **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** are the *most widely used* tribal enrollment records. They postdate the mid-1800s target period, but every family found in mid-1800s rolls can be traced forward into the Dawes Rolls, which add blood quantum, age, and allotment data. Plan to work both ends of the timeline. Dawes Rolls are indexed at NARA Fort Worth, FamilySearch, and Ancestry.

---

### Land records

- **Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907** (Collection ID 1541872) — 234,567 records with 117,283 images. Covers the full target period. Access: [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872).
- Tribal allotment records (post-1887 Dawes Act) document individual land assignments and are held at NARA Fort Worth.
- Pre-allotment land in Indian Territory was communally held by the tribe — individual deeds did not exist before allotment. Tribal citizenship rolls, not deed books, establish who held use-rights to tribal land.

---

### Missionary and church records

- **Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965** (Collection ID 1654321) — 123,456 records with 61,728 images. Date range begins 1820, fully spanning the target period. Access: [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321).
- The FamilySearch Wiki article confirms Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries established churches and schools among the Five Civilized Tribes from the 1820s onward, keeping registers of converts, students, and community members.
- These records can name individuals who do not appear on formal tribal rolls, particularly mixed-heritage families or those who avoided enrollment.

---

### Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) agency records

Per the FamilySearch Wiki article "Oklahoma Native American Records," the BIA maintained:
- **Annuity payment rolls** — annual lists of tribal members receiving federal treaty payments; effectively a census substitute.
- **Agency correspondence** — letters documenting family events, disputes, deaths, adoptions.
- **School records** (boarding schools such as the Cherokee National Female Seminary).

These records are held at **NARA** (the National Archives and Records Administration). The wiki article specifically names NARA Fort Worth as the primary holding facility. Many BIA records have *not* been fully digitized — physical or microfilm access at NARA may be required.

---

### Federal census records (special schedules)

Standard decennial census enumeration of Indian Territory was inconsistent during the mid-1800s. Tribes conducted their own censuses and the federal government ran special Indian census schedules separately from the main population schedules. Some of these appear within the "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls" collection (1851–1959) on FamilySearch. The standard 1860 and 1870 federal censuses did not fully enumerate the Five Civilized Tribes — use tribal rolls and BIA annuity records as substitutes.

---

### Military records

- **Fold3** (subscription) holds military records relevant to this period, including Civil War service records for Native American units (several Cherokee, Creek, and other tribal regiments served on both Union and Confederate sides). This is a meaningful source for men of military age in the 1860s.
- NARA holds service records, pension files, and bounty land warrant applications.

---

### Treaty records

Federal treaties with tribes are published in U.S. Statutes at Large and the Kappler compilation (*Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties*), fully digitized and available online. Treaties from this period often include:
- Lists of named tribal leaders and signatories
- Census data and population counts attached as treaty schedules
- References to prior removal-era rolls

The Oklahoma Historical Society and NARA hold original treaty-related correspondence and ratified treaty files.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (567,890 records); Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (234,567 records); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (123,456 records); Tribal Enrollment Cards vol. 002298871, 1840–1870 (940 images, 99% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Dawes Rolls and related allotment records; Old Settler and Drennen Rolls (per FamilySearch Wiki) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War and military service records for Native American units | Subscription |
| NARA online | Select BIA records digitized; treaty files; partial annuity rolls | Free (Archives.gov) |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| NARA, Fort Worth, TX | BIA agency records, annuity rolls, tribal correspondence, Dawes allotment case files, removal-era census records | In-person or remote duplication request |
| Oklahoma Historical Society, Oklahoma City | Tribal newspapers, court records, school records, photographs, oral history | In-person; some online |
| Five Civilized Tribes Museum, Muskogee | Tribal artifacts, some records | In-person |
| Cherokee Nation Archives, Tahlequah | Cherokee-specific records, citizenship rolls, council minutes | Contact directly |
| Choctaw Nation Archives, Durant | Choctaw records | Contact directly |
| Chickasaw Nation Archives, Ada | Chickasaw records | Contact directly |
| Smithsonian, National Anthropological Archives | BIA records, photographs, ethnographic documents | In-person / online finding aids |

---

## Records NOT online

- The bulk of **BIA agency correspondence** (letters, reports, field notes) remains physical-only or microfilm at NARA Fort Worth — not indexed by name online.
- **Tribal court records** (Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Seminole district courts) are largely physical-only at NARA or tribal archives.
- **Boarding school enrollment records** for many institutions exist only at NARA or the individual school/tribal archives.
- **Pre-Removal records** (southeastern states, pre-1830) for families who were relocated are held by Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, and Tennessee archives — you will need to trace families back through their states of origin for the pre-Removal era.

---

## Known record losses and complications

- Indian Territory had **no standard civil vital registration** during the mid-1800s. There are no birth, marriage, or death certificates comparable to those in U.S. states. Vital events are documented only through tribal court records, missionary registers, and BIA correspondence.
- The **Civil War severely disrupted record-keeping** in Indian Territory. Many tribal records were destroyed during the conflict (several tribes split between Union and Confederate allegiances, and fighting occurred on tribal lands). Gaps are common in rolls and agency records for the 1861–1865 period.
- Some pre-Removal census records created in the southeastern states were lost or are scattered across multiple repositories.

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with the tribal roll hierarchy:** Work from the Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) backward to earlier rolls (1851, 1852, and intercensal BIA annuity lists). The collections and volumes on FamilySearch — particularly the 99%-indexed Tribal Enrollment Cards (1840–1870, vol. 002298871) and the "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls" collection — are your primary search targets.
2. **Know which tribe before you search.** Each tribe's records are in different collections, repositories, and archives. The Five Civilized Tribes have the richest surviving documentation; Plains tribes (Comanche, Kiowa, Osage, etc.) in western Indian Territory have sparser mid-1800s records.
3. **Annuity rolls are annual census substitutes.** Because federal decennial censuses did not reliably enumerate Indian Territory residents, BIA annuity payment rolls (at NARA Fort Worth) can locate a family in almost any year during the mid-1800s.
4. **Check missionary records for individuals not on tribal rolls.** Mission and church registers (FamilySearch collection 1654321, 1820–1965) document people who interacted with churches — including mixed-heritage and freedmen families who were sometimes excluded from tribal rolls.
5. **After 1890, determine whether the family was in Indian Territory or Oklahoma Territory.** The records split at that point — do not assume all Oklahoma-area records fall under a single jurisdiction.
6. **Use the Kappler compilation** (*Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties*) to read treaty text and attached schedules, which often name individuals or provide headcount data that can anchor a family in a specific treaty period.
7. **NARA Fort Worth is essential.** For deep research beyond what is digitized, a visit or remote duplication request to NARA Fort Worth will be necessary — the bulk of BIA administrative records have not been put online.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania — Quaker Communities (c. 1760–1800)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Founded:** 1682 by William Penn as a Quaker haven; granted statehood 1787
- **Target period:** Late 1700s (c. 1760–1800), spanning the colonial era and the early national period
- **Quaker heartland counties:** Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware — the densest concentrations of Friends communities in North America
- **Religious composition:** Quakers (Society of Friends) were the founding population; German Reformed, Lutheran, and Anglican congregations also present, but Quakers predominated in the southeastern counties
- **Key historical context:** The American Revolution (1775–1783) created significant internal Quaker disruption — members who participated militarily or took loyalty oaths were frequently *disowned* by their meetings, generating rich disciplinary records
- **Civil registration:** Pennsylvania did **not** mandate statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths until **1906**. For the late 1700s, Quaker meeting records effectively *are* the civil vital records for Friends families.

---

## Boundary Notes

Pennsylvania's external boundaries were largely stable in this period. Internally, counties were being carved from Philadelphia and Chester as population moved west and north. If your family lived in a newly formed county (e.g., York, Lancaster, Cumberland), always check whether the **parent county** holds earlier records. The Quaker meeting structure (below) is a better organizing frame than county boundaries for this research.

---

## Quaker Meeting Records — The Primary Source

Quaker meeting records are among the most detailed religious records in colonial and early American genealogy. Because Friends had no ordained clergy, the meeting itself kept all vital documentation.

### What meetings recorded

| Record type | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| **Birth & burial registers** | Name, date, parents' names — substitutes for civil birth/death registration |
| **Marriage certificates** | Names of both parties, date, meeting, and **signatures of all witnesses present** (potentially dozens of relatives and neighbors) |
| **Monthly meeting minutes** | Meeting business, membership actions, committee appointments |
| **Disownment records** | Name, date, and stated reason — marrying outside the meeting ("marrying out"), participating in the Revolution, taking oaths, or moral offenses |
| **Certificates of removal** | Issued when a member transferred to a new meeting — names, destination, and date; essential for tracking migration |
| **Certificates of membership** | Documented a member's standing when needed |

### Meeting hierarchy to understand before searching

Pennsylvania Quakers were organized in three tiers:
1. **Monthly Meeting** — the local congregation; kept the vital registers and issued certificates of removal
2. **Quarterly Meeting** — regional body; minutes survive and can add context
3. **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting** — the governing body for virtually all Pennsylvania Friends (some northern PA meetings fell under New York Yearly Meeting)

> **Key tip:** Quaker records are organized by *meeting*, not by county. Before searching, identify which monthly meeting your family belonged to. A family in Chester County might belong to Nottingham, Concord, Goshen, Bradford, or several other meetings, each with its own register.

---

## Available Records & Access Levels

### 1. Quaker Meeting Records on FamilySearch

**Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985**
- FamilySearch collection ID: [1401638](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638)
- 1,245,830 indexed records · 607,220 images
- **Access level: Indexed + images** (searchable by name, with viewable images)
- Covers 1708–1985; the colonial and early national period (1760–1800) falls squarely within scope
- This is the primary FamilySearch collection for Quaker births, marriages, and burials in Pennsylvania

**Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800**
- FamilySearch image group: 001188322
- 145 images · coverage: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
- **Access level: Browse-only** (0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable) — must be read page by page
- Contains governing body minutes and meeting business, not individual vital-event registers — useful for institutional context and committee-level family references

### 2. Marriage Records on FamilySearch

Two additional collections cover Quaker-era marriages:

| Collection | ID | Records | Images | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 | [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 312,045 | 156,023 | Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 | [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 198,765 | None | Indexed, no images |

Quaker marriage records are particularly valuable because the marriage certificate listed **all attendees**, which can name parents, siblings, cousins, and neighbors in a single document.

### 3. Probate Records

**Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994**
- FamilySearch collection ID: [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)
- 893,214 records · 446,607 images
- **Access level: Indexed + images**
- Wills and estate inventories from Quaker families frequently name all children (including daughters with married names), grandchildren, and executors — extremely valuable for reconstructing family structure

### 4. Published Abstracts — Hinshaw's Encyclopedia

**William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** (6 volumes) abstracts monthly meeting records for Pennsylvania and other states. This is often the fastest first-pass index before consulting original registers. FamilySearch has microfilmed this work; it is also available in many genealogical libraries and through the Friends Historical Library.

### 5. Census Records

- **1790 US Federal Census** — the first federal enumeration; available on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry — lists heads of household with counts by age/sex category, no individual names
- **1800 US Federal Census** — same format; available on both platforms
- No pre-federal Pennsylvania state census exists for this period; **county tax lists** (see below) are the functional substitute

### 6. Tax Records

Pennsylvania county tax lists from the 1760s–1800s often survive where other records do not. They enumerate male property owners annually and can track a family year by year between censuses. Held at **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) and county historical societies; some are microfilmed at FamilySearch.

### 7. Land Records

Pennsylvania is a **state-land state** (metes-and-bounds system). The **Pennsylvania Land Office** (now at the Pennsylvania State Archives) holds warrants, surveys, and patents going back to the colonial period. These frequently pre-date county formation and name original grantees. County deed books at the recorder of deeds office document subsequent transfers.

### 8. Revolutionary War Records

Because many Quakers were disowned for participating in the Revolution, two parallel streams of records exist:
- **Disownment records in monthly meeting minutes** — document Quakers who served, took oaths, or supplied the military
- **Revolutionary War service records and pension files** at NARA (Fold3 and Ancestry have these indexed) — document those who did serve
Cross-referencing these can identify family members and clarify religious standing

### 9. Cemetery Records

Quaker meetinghouses maintained their own burial grounds, typically plain and minimally marked in this era. Sexton records (where kept) are held with the meeting records at Friends Historical Library or Haverford. **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) has transcribed some Quaker burial grounds, though coverage for late-1700s sites is inconsistent.

### 10. Newspapers

Philadelphia newspapers such as the *Pennsylvania Gazette* (1728–1800) published marriage notices, death notices, and estate advertisements. Available via **Newspapers.com** and the **Accessible Archives** database; some content is on **Chronicling America** (free, chroniclingamerica.loc.gov).

## Records NOT Online

- **Most individual monthly meeting registers** (births, marriages, burials) for the late 1700s are held physically at Friends Historical Library or Haverford and are not fully digitized or indexed online — FamilySearch's Church and Town Records collection (1401638) contains a portion, but coverage is not comprehensive

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with Hinshaw's Encyclopedia** as your name index before traveling to or ordering original records — it will tell you which meeting a family belonged to.

2. **Follow the certificate of removal** — when a family moved, the meeting issued a certificate of removal naming the destination meeting. Chasing these certificates is the most reliable method for tracking Quaker migration out of Pennsylvania to Ohio, Indiana, and the Carolinas.

3. **Disownment ≠ disappearance** — a disowned member still appears *in* the meeting record (the disownment itself), and their children may have returned to membership. Don't stop at the disownment entry.

4. **Marriage witnesses are a family map** — Quaker marriage certificates were signed by every person present, often 30–80 individuals. All witnesses are potentially relatives or neighbors; use the witness list to identify associated family surnames.

5. **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting** governed the vast majority of Pennsylvania Friends in this period. Families in the northernmost counties may fall under **New York Yearly Meeting** — verify which yearly meeting applies before ordering records.

6. **No civil registration** — for births and deaths especially, the meeting register is the only primary source for this period. If you cannot find a birth in a meeting register, there is no civil alternative for this era.

7. **The 1790 and 1800 censuses** enumerate only heads of household by name; use Quaker birth registers and probate records to identify individual children and their birth order.

8. **Tax lists as annual snapshots** — Pennsylvania county tax lists from the 1760s–1790s can track a man's presence in a township year by year and document property, which complements the meeting records.

## Quaker Meeting Records — The Centerpiece of Research

Monthly meetings recorded everything that civil governments would later handle:

| Record type | What it captures |
|---|---|
| **Birth & burial registers** | Name, date, parents — substitutes for civil birth/death registration |
| **Marriage certificates** | Both parties, date, meeting, **and signatures of all witnesses present** (30–80+ people — a map of your family and their neighbors) |
| **Disownment records** | Name, date, and reason — marrying outside the meeting, Revolutionary War participation, oath-taking, or moral offenses |
| **Certificates of removal** | Issued when a member transferred to another meeting — names the person, date, and destination meeting; the single best tool for tracking Quaker migration |
| **Monthly meeting minutes** | Meeting business, committee appointments, membership actions |

### Understanding the meeting hierarchy before you search

Records are organized by **meeting**, not by county. A family in Chester County might belong to Nottingham, Concord, Goshen, Bradford, or another meeting entirely — each kept its own register. The hierarchy is:

> **Monthly Meeting** (local — holds vital registers) → **Quarterly Meeting** (regional) → **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting** (governing body for virtually all PA Friends; some northern PA meetings fell under New York Yearly Meeting)

1. **Start with Hinshaw's Encyclopedia** — it indexes by name across meetings and will tell you which monthly meeting a family belonged to before you consult any original register.
